Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 creates the Generative AI Governing Board to oversee the ethical and effective use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) by Commonwealth of Pennsylvania agencies.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 requires agencies to apply core values such as accuracy, adaptability, equity, innovation, mission alignment, privacy, proportionality, safety, security, and transparency in using Generative AI technologies.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 charges the Office of Administration (OA) with developing policies to ensure responsible AI use, including auditing outputs for accuracy and protecting user privacy.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 instructs the Board to recommend guidelines and assess agency requests to utilize Generative AI, ensuring adherence to core values, bias testing, and aligning applications with governmental missions.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 composes the Board of key government officials and mandates monthly meetings.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 encourages collaboration with external AI experts and stakeholders for feedback on AI usage.

Pennsylvania Executive Order 2023-19 orders OA to provide training for employees on using Generative AI tools effectively.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 establishes six core AI Values that District of Columbia agencies must assess before deploying AI tools, specifically focusing on benefits, safety, accountability, transparency, sustainability, and privacy.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 forms an AI Advisory Group and an AI Taskforce to align AI Values, conduct community engagement, support governance, and advise the Mayor on AI use.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 instructs the Office of the Chief Technology Officer, Department of Human Resources, and other agencies to develop privacy, cybersecurity, recruitment, and procurement benchmarks by specified deadlines.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 requires agencies to submit AI strategic plans addressing potential improvements, risks, and stakeholder engagement by designated dates.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 charges the AI Taskforce with providing technical advice, reporting on progress, and ensuring compliance with strategic benchmarks.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 mandates that the Advisory Group and AI Taskforce sunset on December 31, 2026.

DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028 requires these bodies to provide ongoing guidance, review AI tools, and align technology use with the District's stated AI Values.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) establishes the New York State Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Automation Commission to study and determine regulations for AI, robotics, and automation.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) tasks the commission with examining current state laws, comparative policies, liability issues, employment impact, confidentiality, restrictions on AI weaponry use, regulatory impacts on the technology industry, and public sector AI applications.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) comprises thirteen members appointed by state government officials and university chancellors.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) authorizes the commission to conduct hearings and gather testimonies to thoroughly analyze relevant AI issues.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) requires the commission to publish a final report for state leadership at least thirty days before the act's expiration.

New York Senate Bill S3971B (2019) sets the act's expiration and repeal date as December 31, 2020.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) define "assessment mechanism" to include AI and technology used for remote or in-person eye assessments.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) require such mechanisms to offer patient-provider interaction, gather patient history, and acknowledge limitations, including not replacing in-person exams or issuing initial contact lens prescriptions.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) instruct providers using assessment mechanisms to adhere to traditional care standards, verify patient identity and age, ensure recent in-person exams, and maintain patient records.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) establish that using eye assessment data alone for prescriptions is prohibited, and providers must certify prescriptions with their signature and license.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) impose civil penalties up to $10,000 for violations, with rights to hearings and appeals.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) authorize the department of health to implement rules and regulations for enforcement.

Rhode Island SB 2083 (2022) include severability to maintain chapter validity if parts are invalidated.

Utah SB 96 establishes a Deep Technology Talent Initiative to develop and oversee funding for programs related to deep technology, including artificial intelligence.

Utah SB 96 requires institutions of higher education to collaborate with employers to create programs that address workforce needs in deep technology sectors.

Utah SB 96 mandates submission and review of program proposals by institutions seeking funding, emphasizing workforce relevance, partnerships, and the integration of deep technology skills.

Utah SB 96 instructs the Deep Technology Talent Advisory Council to prioritize and recommend proposals for funding based on specified criteria including workforce impact and cost-effectiveness.

Utah SB 96 allocates $5 million from the Workforce Development Restricted Account to the Deep Technology Talent Initiative for fiscal year 2021.

Utah SB 96 requires annual reports from funded programs on performance and outcomes, which the board must submit to relevant legislative committees.

Utah SB 96 defines the composition and responsibilities of the Deep Technology Talent Advisory Council in supporting the initiatives.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." defines "high technology manufacturing businesses" to include entities involved in manufacturing activities incorporating artificial intelligence, autonomous vehicles, drones, and related AI-operated machinery.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." allows these businesses a tax credit against state taxes equal to 100% of the tax attributable to their qualified investment in expanding or establishing AI-related operations, providing they create at least 20 new jobs within 12 months.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." ensures that the median compensation for these new jobs exceeds $45,000, adjusted annually for inflation.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." precludes businesses claiming this credit from simultaneously claiming other tax credits for the same investment.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." empowers the commissioner to establish rules and require notices for monitoring the application and eligibility of the credit.

West Virginia HB 2760 (2021), Sec 11-13Q "Credit allowed for specified high technology manufacturers." tasks the commissioner with overseeing compliance and verifying ongoing eligibility for the credit throughout the 20-year period.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) directs the Office of Regulatory Management, with the Chief Information Officer and relevant Secretariats, to establish AI usage standards for Virginia's state government.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) requires reviewing laws and regulations affecting AI, including privacy and intellectual property laws, to ensure public protection.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) ensures AI usage is transparent, secure, and impartial with adequate privacy safeguards.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) recommends uniform AI standards across state agencies, including education and IT guidelines.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) collaborates with educational institutions to integrate AI in curricula and promote responsible AI usage in learning environments.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) prepares students and the workforce for careers involving AI through partnerships with colleges and industry.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) identifies opportunities for AI to enhance state government efficiency and ethical decision-making.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) explores AI's economic impacts, encouraging industry innovation and supporting displaced workers.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) works with the Virginia Department of Energy to assess AI's impact on power requirements.

Virginia Executive Directive 5 (2023) requires completion of these actions and recommendations by December 15, 2023.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 orders WaTech, with cabinet agencies, to report on generative AI initiatives by September 2024, assessing feasibility, benefits, and challenges.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 directs WaTech and DES to issue guidelines for AI procurement focusing on safety, equity, and privacy by September 2024.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 requires DES and WaTech to develop an AI training plan for government workers by January 2025.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 instructs WaTech to create guidelines for AI's community impact, focusing on equity and algorithmic bias by December 2024.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 mandates DES and WaTech to update procurement templates to include equity and risk considerations by January 2025.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 tasks the Office of Equity to develop an accountability framework for AI equity and ethics by September 2024.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 ensures WaTech provides risk assessment guidance for high-risk AI systems by December 2024.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 commands the State Human Resources Division to assess AI's workforce impact and mitigate negative effects by December 2024.

Washington Executive Order 24-01 charges the Workforce Training Board with fostering AI education and research by January 2025.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) regulates the use of automated or virtual assessment mechanisms, including AI devices, for conducting eye assessments, requiring interaction between the patient and a licensed provider.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) requires the collection of medical history and previous prescriptions and mandates acceptance of certain disclosures about the limitations of such assessments.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) specifies that an assessment mechanism cannot issue initial prescriptions for contact lenses or their renewals without a prior in-person examination within 24 months.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) obliges providers to follow the standard of eye care, verify patient identity and age, and confirm recent in-person examinations before issuing prescriptions.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) imposes a civil penalty up to $10,000 for violations, enforceable by the department of health or attorney general, with rights to an administrative hearing and appeal.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) instructs the department of health to create necessary rules and regulations.

Rhode Island HB 6654 (2022) ensures severability of the act’s provisions if any part is invalidated by a court.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) define "artificial intelligence," "generative AI," "deepfake," and "state agency" in relation to AI governance.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) apply provisions to all state agency computer systems, with exceptions for research and personal use systems.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) prohibit uses by state agencies for classifying individuals leading to discrimination, surveillance in public spaces without a warrant, and malicious use of deepfakes.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) allow AI use with human oversight on irreversible decisions, disclosure of AI-generated content, and informing users of AI interactions.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) require state agencies to review AI use, modify inconsistent procedures, and document compliance within nine months, reporting to the department of information technology.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) mandate annual reporting and updates on AI system compliance and procurement to key government officials and public posting on the department website.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) sever provisions to ensure remaining regulations remain in effect if parts are invalidated.

New Hampshire H1688 (2024) enact the chapter on July 1, 2024.

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 creates an inventory of automated decision systems used by the government, emphasizing AI's role within human processes, to be maintained by the Division of Artificial Intelligence under the Agency of Digital Services (ADS).

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 requires annual updates and reviews for the inventory's accuracy and completeness.

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 recommends various remediation measures for systems showing problematic behavior, including process changes upstream or downstream, modifications to the AI, or decommissioning problematic systems.

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 advises narrowing the inventory’s scope to focus on AI systems that pose potential risks rather than encompassing all apps and tools.

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 highlights the importance of ongoing outcome monitoring over third-party bias testing, advising additional tracking elements for monitoring results and applied remediation.

Vermont Agency of Digital Services Report regarding Inventory of Artificial Intelligence Usage, pursuant to 3 V.S.A. § 3305 proposes focusing on AI system autonomy rather than their decision-making capability, urging identification of agencies directly utilizing these systems.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 outlines the acceptable use of generative AI by Executive Branch Cabinet and Non-Cabinet Agencies in Kansas, emphasizing safety, privacy, and intellectual property protection.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 requires entities to review AI-generated content for accuracy, appropriateness, privacy, and security before dissemination.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 prohibits verbatim use of AI-generated content, reliance on it for final decisions or official statements, and impersonation of individuals or organizations.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 forbids input of Restricted Use Information, inappropriate, copyrighted, or proprietary material into AI systems.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 directs agencies to require contractors to disclose AI usage in contracts and prohibits use of state confidential data without approval.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 allows software code from AI only after risk mitigation and mandates annotation.

Kansas Policy and Procedures Memorandum 8200.00 tasks agency heads with procedural compliance and the Office of Information Technology Services (OITS) with policy maintenance.

Maryland 2020 HB49 require jurisdictions using pretrial risk scoring instruments for determining defendants' pretrial release eligibility to conduct independent validation studies of these tools at least once every three to five years.

Maryland 2020 HB49 establish a Pretrial Services Program Grant Fund to provide grants to eligible counties for creating or improving pretrial services programs, or for conducting validations of pretrial risk scoring instruments as per § 5–103 of the Criminal Procedure Article.

Maryland 2020 HB49 require eligible counties applying for grants to provide a description of how their programs meet requirements and information deemed necessary by the Executive Director of the Governor’s Office of Crime Control and Prevention.

Maryland 2020 HB49 ensure pretrial services programs use validated, evidence-based, race-neutral risk scoring instruments following Maryland Rules, apply effective best practices, and incorporate multiple levels of supervision based on defendant risk scores, including technological and treatment provisions.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 establishes a special commission to study the impact of automation and artificial intelligence on the workforce, businesses, and the economy.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 charges the commission with ensuring sustainable jobs, fair benefits, and workplace safety standards.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 instructs the commission to study trends in industry transformation and impacts on workers, including access to healthcare and benefits.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 collaborates with the executive office of labor and workforce development to track industry trends and research best practices for the future of work.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 requires the commission to gather data from various sectors, work with training organizations, and hold public hearings across different regions.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 directs the commission to file a report by September 1, 2021, with analysis, recommendations, and potential legislation for securing worker benefits and updating workforce training.

Massachusetts (2020) House Bill 5250, Section 92 ensures recommendations include support for lifelong learning, skill development, and integration of new technologies in workforce training.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) urges platforms generating and disseminating deepfake and cheapfake media to voluntarily commit to preventing and removing harmful content.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) defines deepfakes as media that appears to depict authentic speech or conduct through substantial technical means, and cheapfakes as any software-generated audiovisual alteration.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) notes that generative AI platforms can anticipate and prevent the creation of harmful content, with social media and content-sharing forums capable of taking steps to remove such media.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) recognizes the potential negative impact, including impersonation, fraud, and political misinformation, while acknowledging the promise of AI if used responsibly.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) encourages the development of AI accountability and transparency standards, following examples set by the federal government and other states.

New Jersey Assembly Resolution 141 (2024) calls for New Jersey to become a leader in responsible media technology through these voluntary commitments.

Louisiana SCR 49 urges the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity to study the impact of artificial intelligence on operations, procurement, and policy in Louisiana.

Louisiana SCR 49 requires the committee to submit a written report of its findings to the House Committee on Commerce and the Senate Committee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and International Affairs at least sixty days before the 2024 Regular Session.

Louisiana SCR 49 instructs the report to propose recommendations and legislative proposals to aid government and businesses in leveraging AI benefits while protecting consumers.

Louisiana SCR 49 encourages the committee to seek input from the Department of Economic Development, the office of technology services, Division of Administration, the Department of Justice, and industry partners.

Louisiana SCR 49 transmits a copy of the resolution to the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 requests the Joint Legislative Committee on Technology and Cybersecurity to study and make recommendations concerning the use and regulation of artificial intelligence.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 instructs the joint committee to solicit data and testimony from relevant persons, entities, agencies, and institutions.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 requires the joint committee to make annual reports with policy recommendations to the legislature.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 recognizes the multifaceted potential threats of artificial intelligence in education, criminal justice, finance, health, welfare, and state fiscal health.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 acknowledges the potential for beneficial uses of artificial intelligence to improve government operations and service efficiency.

Louisiana (2024) HCR 66 emphasizes the necessity for more information before developing policies to maximize AI benefits and minimize its misuse in the state of Louisiana.

Rhode Island House Resolution 6423 requests the Department of Administration and the RI Division of Information Technology report on the extent of algorithmic decision-making used by the State of Rhode Island.

Rhode Island House Resolution 6423 tasks them with assessing the validation, testing, and evaluation of automated decision systems, especially regarding biases such as racial and gender biases.

Rhode Island House Resolution 6423 instructs them to provide recommendations on regulatory or legislative action regarding the use of automated decision systems by state offices, compliance with data protection laws, and timelines for the implementation of AI technologies.

Rhode Island House Resolution 6423 requires delivery of this information to the House of Representatives and the Chair of the House Committee on Innovation, Internet, and Technology by September 29, 2023.

Rhode Island House Resolution 6423 authorizes the Secretary of State to transmit certified copies of this resolution to relevant state officials.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) recognizes the potential impact of robotics, automation, and AI on the workforce and the importance of planning for their effects.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) requires Delaware State Agencies and government branches to implement daily operational and long-term strategic planning to mitigate negative impacts of these technologies.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) encourages consideration of legal and ethical implications in AI development without hindering innovation.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) emphasizes the need for AI applications to prioritize security, ethics, dignity, autonomy, and self-determination.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) highlights the risk of technological displacement and its effects on public and private sectors.

Delaware House Concurrent Resolution 7 (2019-2020) aims to prepare Delaware for changes in employment due to advancements in AI and automation.

New York City Council No. 1806-A requires each New York City agency to report annually to the mayor’s office of operations or a designated entity by December 31 on all algorithmic tools used in the prior year.

New York City Council No. 1806-A defines "algorithmic tool" as technologies derived from AI, machine learning, or predictive analytics that impact public rights, services, and resource allocation.

New York City Council No. 1806-A instructs agencies to provide tool names, purposes, data types and sources, usage descriptions, vendor details, and start dates.

New York City Council No. 1806-A directs the mayor’s office to compile this information and report it to the mayor and the council speaker by March 31, sorted by agency.

New York City Council No. 1806-A prohibits disclosure of any information that violates laws, endangers safety, or interferes with investigations.

New York City Council No. 1806-A implements the law with immediate effect.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 requires the Department of Administration to biennially inventory AI systems for consequential decisions used by state agencies, detailing system names, vendors, capabilities, and impact assessments, and publish results online.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 obligates state agency heads to conduct impact assessments every two years for AI systems, analyzing efficacy, oversight, accountability, risks, effects on individuals, and compliance with anti-discrimination measures, with results also published online.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 prohibits state agencies from using AI systems involving biometric identification, emotion recognition, cognitive manipulation, social scoring, and those using data hosted in specified foreign countries.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 restricts state agencies' data transfer without consent and requires multi-factor authentication for contracted AI systems.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 directs the department to establish regulations for AI system governance, require pre-implementation assessments, and prevent discriminatory impacts.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 allows individuals to sue for damages resulting from violations related to AI use.

Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019) requires employers in Illinois to notify job applicants if artificial intelligence will analyze their video interviews and to provide information on how the AI works, including characteristics it evaluates.

Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019) requires employers to obtain applicants' consent before using AI to evaluate them.

Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019) prohibits employers from using AI analysis on applicants who do not consent.

Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019) permits sharing of applicant videos only with individuals necessary for evaluating the applicant's fitness for the position.

Illinois House Bill 2557 (2019) obliges employers to delete video interviews and instruct any recipients to do the same, including backup copies, within 30 days if the applicant requests it.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 require individuals who know or should know that a communication includes a deepfake depicting a candidate or political party, intended to deceive voters, to include a specific disclosure statement: "This communication has been manipulated or generated by artificial intelligence."

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 mandate that the statement be audible in audio communications and visible throughout the entirety of print, video, or digital communications.

Alaska Senate Bill No. 177 define "deepfake" as an image, audio, or video created or manipulated with complex computational techniques to create a realistic yet false depiction of an individual, potentially altering a reasonable person's understanding of their appearance, conduct, or words compared to the original media.

Illinois House Bill 53 (2021) amends the Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act by requiring employers using AI to analyze video interviews for in-person interview selection to collect demographic data.

Illinois House Bill 53 (2021) requires the collection of race and ethnicity data of applicants selected and not selected for interviews, as well as of those hired.

Illinois House Bill 53 (2021) obligates employers to report this demographic data annually to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity by December 31.

Illinois House Bill 53 (2021) requires the Department to analyze this data and determine any racial bias in the AI use.

Illinois House Bill 53 (2021) instructs the Department to report findings of racial bias to the Governor and General Assembly by July 1 each year.

West Virginia House Resolution 3 establishes a Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence within the West Virginia House of Delegates.

West Virginia House Resolution 3 comprises up to eleven members appointed by the Speaker of the House.

West Virginia House Resolution 3 tasks the committee with receiving testimony, considering legislation, and recommending action on AI-related issues in the state.

West Virginia House Resolution 3 subjects the committee to the House rules governing Standing Committees, where applicable.

Hawaii House Concurrent Resolution 71 request the Department of Health to convene a Stakeholder Working Group to study language access in health care settings, focusing on the benefits and impacts of technologies such as artificial intelligence.

Hawaii House Concurrent Resolution 71 instruct the Working Group to assess experiences of limited English proficiency (LEP) populations, existing language services, and disparities in health care access.

Hawaii House Concurrent Resolution 71 advise the Group to make recommendations for enhancing meaningful access to health care, including options for utilizing AI-based solutions.

Hawaii House Concurrent Resolution 71 require the Department of Health to invite stakeholders, including LEP individuals, health care providers, insurers, community-based organizations, and language service providers to participate in the Group.

Hawaii House Concurrent Resolution 71 instruct the Department of Health to submit a report of the Group's findings and recommendations, along with proposed legislation, to the Legislature by a specified deadline.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) authorizes the State Department of Education to implement a K-12 computer science curriculum based on 2018 standards, including artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) instructs the State Department of Education to collaborate with the Center for Cyber Education at Mississippi State University for curriculum development.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) requires school districts, starting in the 2022-2023 school year, to ensure all middle schools offer computer science instruction and 50% of elementary schools provide a minimum of one hour weekly.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) mandates charter schools serving middle and high school students to offer computer science courses.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) starting in the 2023-2024 school year, directs 50% of high schools to provide computer science courses and all elementary schools to offer at least one hour of exploratory computer science weekly.

Mississippi House Bill 633 (2021) ensures, beginning the 2024-2025 school year, computer science instruction is available in all schools within each district.

Vermont 2019 Act No.16, Section 20 amends the meeting limitations of the Artificial Intelligence Task Force to permit no more than 15 meetings, excluding public hearings for obtaining public testimony on AI.

Vermont 2019 Act No.16, Section 20 requires the Task Force to submit an update by February 15, 2019, to the Senate Committee on Government Operations and the House Committee on Energy and Technology.

Vermont 2019 Act No.16, Section 20 requires the Task Force to submit a final report by January 15, 2020, to the same committees, detailing their findings and recommendations related to AI.

Vermont 2019 Act No.16, Section 20 specifies that the Task Force will cease to exist on January 15, 2020.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence adopts an ambitious approach to AI-enabled capabilities in defense, aiming for comprehensive exploitation to enhance efficiency and effectiveness.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence emphasizes ethical, legal, and responsible development of AI, incorporating human oversight, particularly in AI-enabled weapons systems.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence addresses key challenges such as algorithmic bias, accountability, unpredictability, and safety concerns to maintain public trust and stakeholder collaboration.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence implements a governance framework involving senior defense officials and specialized units to ensure compliance with national and international laws, including International Humanitarian Law.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence establishes ethical principles focused on human-centricity, responsibility, understanding, bias mitigation, and reliability for AI in defense.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence collaborates with the Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation and forms an AI Ethics Advisory Panel to guide ethical implementation.

AMBITIOUS, SAFE, RESPONSIBLE: Our approach to the delivery of AI-enabled capability in Defence reaffirms commitment against fully autonomous weapon systems, advocating for human control and accountability in AI-empowered defense systems, and participates in international discourse on lethal autonomous weapons systems.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act establishes a stand-alone competitive research and extension grant program under the Department of Agriculture to advance mechanization and automation for specialty crops.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act mandates projects to create or improve cost-effective technologies that reduce manual labor and increase efficiency in crop production, resource management, and processing.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act requires projects to promote the adoption of mechanization and automation technologies by emphasizing factors such as connectivity, autonomy, and cost-effectiveness.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act specifies projects to accelerate automation through prototype development, in-field trials, and rapid commercialization.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act allows grants to be awarded to federal agencies, universities, research institutions, private organizations, and other eligible entities.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act mandates a competitive grant process based on scientific peer review and industry relevance.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act requires annual consultations with the specialty crops committee to review procedures, objectives, and grant awards.

Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act allocates $20 million annually from the Commodity Credit Corporation to fund the program starting fiscal year 2024.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 establishes international artificial intelligence research partnerships between U.S. cities and their international counterparts to promote AI leadership, economic cooperation, and workforce development.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 encourages public-private partnerships, including nonprofits and academic institutions, to support these AI research collaborations.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 requires coordination with the National Science Foundation to align activities with U.S. AI research priorities and leverage existing resources.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 prohibits partnerships with cities in countries deemed a national security concern or detrimental to U.S. foreign policy.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 limits research to non-national security AI areas and mandates adherence to export control regulations.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 authorizes the Secretary of State to enter contracts to facilitate partnerships and allocates $20 million annually from 2025 to 2028 for implementation.

International Artificial Intelligence Research Partnership Act of 2024 mandates annual reporting on partnerships, research scope, city participation, coordination efforts, and implementation challenges to relevant congressional committees.

Expanding AI Voices Act amends the National AI Initiative Act by introducing a new subsection focused on expanding AI capacity.

Expanding AI Voices Act mandates the Director of the National Science Foundation to competitively award eligible higher education institutions and nonprofit organizations to enhance AI research, education, and workforce development.

Expanding AI Voices Act specifies eligibility for institutions not among the top 100 in federal R&D spending, historically Black colleges, minority-serving institutions, Tribal colleges, and their consortia.

Expanding AI Voices Act encourages collaborations with various stakeholders, including AI research institutes and private sector entities.

Expanding AI Voices Act allows use of funds for AI research programs, faculty development, resource access, community building, workshops, and ethical AI education.

Expanding AI Voices Act requires outreach to eligible entities, emphasizing underserved and underrepresented communities.

Expanding AI Voices Act ensures awarded projects complement existing programs without duplication.

Expanding AI Voices Act considers diversity, geographic distribution, and resource constraints in award decisions.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) proposes the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA) to regulate AI in Canada, focusing on high-impact AI systems.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) empowers the Minister of Innovation, Science, and Industry to enforce AIDA, supported by a new AI and Data Commissioner.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) prohibits the reckless and malicious use of AI that causes harm, introducing new criminal law provisions.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) aligns with international norms, such as the EU AI Act, and integrates with existing Canadian laws.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) mandates businesses to identify, assess, and mitigate risks associated with high-impact AI systems.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) requires transparency, fairness, safety, and accountability in AI systems.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) introduces administrative penalties and criminal offences for non-compliance.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) plans a consultation process for the development of regulations, seeking input from stakeholders.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) establishes mechanisms for human oversight and monitoring of AI systems.

Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (Companion document) targets AI systems impacting services, biometric identification, behavior influence, and health and safety.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) establishes Chapter 93M regarding AI accountability and consumer protection in Massachusetts, defining key terms such as algorithmic discrimination and high-risk AI systems.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) mandates developers to identify, mitigate, and disclose risks of algorithmic discrimination, and requires public summaries of AI systems and biases.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) compels deployers of high-risk AI systems to implement risk management programs and conduct annual impact assessments, with mandatory consumer notifications on consequential AI decisions.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) requires corporations to disclose their use of AI in consumer targeting and behavior influence, ensuring transparency and consumer rights protection.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) exempts small businesses, low-risk systems, and federally compliant entities from certain provisions.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) empowers the Attorney General to enforce regulations, categorizing violations under unfair trade practices, while providing a defense for proactive compliance.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) permits rulemaking authority for the Attorney General to set compliance and notification standards and mandates a public education campaign on AI consumer rights.

Massachusetts HD 396 (2025-2026) specifies varying effective dates for sections within 180 days to one year post-passage.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines instructs all City department personnel to thoroughly review and fact-check AI-generated content and disclose AI use in output.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines prohibits entering sensitive information into public Generative AI tools and mandates using AI tools with caution to avoid misleading the public or making inappropriate decisions.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines encourages experimentation with AI tools for drafting and image generation but requires human review and explicit disclosure of AI usage in communications.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines advises IT leaders to track AI use, ensure transparency, and work with vendors to ensure AI components are explainable and auditable.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines requires consulting the Office of Cybersecurity when developing or procuring AI applications.

San Francisco Generative AI Guidelines tasks the City Administrator’s Office with updating guidelines and working with external experts to manage AI risks and protect data, while evolving policies in line with new legislative frameworks.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI establishes statewide governance for AI implementation, emphasizing data protection and quality in Ohio.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI requires state agencies to document and approve AI use cases and submit them to the AI Council for approval.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI mandates testing and ongoing monitoring to prevent bias and errors in AI outputs.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI requires human oversight to verify AI decisions, especially those impacting legal or regulatory areas.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI dictates AI procurement procedures, ensuring security, privacy, and proper data licensing.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI charges the Ohio Department of Administrative Services with developing AI training for state workers, emphasizing ethical considerations and the responsible use of generative AI.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI mandates security and privacy controls, prohibiting the input of sensitive data into generative AI without consent.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI instructs the Chief Data Officer Council to establish data governance for AI, focusing on data integrity and regulation.

State of Ohio Administrative Policy on AI assigns the multi-agency AI Council with overseeing AI use, evaluating societal impacts, and maintaining AI solution repositories.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 establishes an AI Subcabinet to oversee AI use in Maryland state government, fostering principles such as fairness, innovation, privacy, safety, and transparency.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 directs the AI Subcabinet to create an AI Action Plan incorporating NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework to ensure adherence to AI principles.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 instructs the Subcabinet to upskill the state workforce in AI and explore partnerships with external AI talent for targeted projects.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 mandates the study of AI's impact on critical domains, including workforce and economic development, and the provision of recommendations to the Governor and legislature.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 requires the Department of Information Technology to assess infrastructure for safely testing AI prototypes and collaborate with the Department of General Services to create procedures for AI pilots.

Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 ensures AI initiatives align with state and federal laws and does not impair existing authorities, remaining severable if parts are invalidated.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) outlines protocols for the responsible use of AI within Georgia state agencies, focusing on ethics, transparency, and accountability.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) requires agencies to align AI use with legal standards and agency objectives and to report AI tools to the Georgia Technology Authority (GTA).

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) mandates testing and monitoring of AI solutions to ensure safety and accuracy, while addressing ethical, legal, and societal implications.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) specifies guidelines for contracting third-party AI services, emphasizing adherence to GTA and NIST standards and practices for responsible AI.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) instructs agencies to identify and mitigate biases and inaccuracies in AI-generated outputs.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) ensures data protection by adhering to Enterprise's Data Protection Policies and obtaining consent for data use.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) stipulates training and awareness for responsible AI use and a system for reporting AI misuse or unintended impacts.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) requires rigorous testing and ongoing monitoring for AI development and collaboration.

Georgia Technology Authority Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use (SS-23-002) allows State CIO or GTA OIS to terminate the use of AI tools posing risks.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 establishes the Governor’s Task Force on Generative Artificial Intelligence to evaluate and promote the responsible use of GenAI in Alabama's executive-branch agencies.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 requires the Task Force to submit a report by November 30, 2024, detailing GenAI use, risks, and recommendations for its governance framework within state government, including data management, model monitoring, and human oversight.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 instructs each state executive-branch agency to submit an inventory of their GenAI use by May 1, 2024, detailing vendor information, capabilities, and safety measures.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 directs the Office of Information Technology to establish a secure cloud infrastructure for GenAI pilot projects, encouraging state agencies to test and utilize GenAI responsibly.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 encourages state executive-branch agencies to explore GenAI applications in collaboration with experts for improving government services and employee performance.

Alabama Executive Order No. 738 specifies that the order affects executive-branch entities and does not create private enforceable rights.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy requires entities in North Dakota’s executive branch to ensure AI technologies are reliable, valid, and transparent, with clear explanations of AI use and marked AI decision-making involving medium to high-risk data.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy mandates accountability for secure AI development, compliance with laws and standards, and prohibits using state-managed passwords for third-party apps.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy incorporates NDIT’s Security Risk Management Program in AI operations, mandates regular risk assessments, and restricts inputting moderate/high-risk data into public AI/ML services.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy requires NDIT to offer AI training and workshops, maintain an AI technology inventory, and ensure entities use vetted technologies.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy demands compliance with data protection laws, ethical AI use, and fairness without bias.

State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy stipulates AI must adhere to legal standards, including copyright, with review of licensing agreements and recognition that AI-generated content lacks copyright protection.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework establishes the North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework to ensure ethical AI application across state agencies.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework requires state agencies to follow guidelines which emphasize human-centered AI with oversight ensuring AI use benefits citizens without negatively impacting rights or access to services.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework stipulates transparency, requiring agencies to notify individuals of AI use and its impacts in accessible language.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework mandates robust security measures, ongoing monitoring, and risk assessments to ensure the safety and effectiveness of AI systems.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework demands strict data privacy controls throughout AI lifecycle stages and promotes equitable AI development free from biases.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework insists on accountability where agencies must audit AI use and provide necessary training to personnel.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework empowers staff through AI training to maximize public service effectiveness.

North Carolina State Government Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Framework requires agencies to maintain an AI inventory, report it for transparency, and conduct risk assessments using NIST AI RMF guided by state offices for comprehensive risk management.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy requires all New Hampshire State Employees to adhere to ethical guidelines for AI use, emphasizing protection of Personal Identifying Information (PII) and sensitive data.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy dictates a human-centric approach, transparency, fairness, privacy, and continuous monitoring in AI deployment for government services.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy allows AI for decision support, public engagement, predictive analytics, image and video analysis, natural language processing, generative content, healthcare, environmental monitoring, and transportation, subject to stringent data protection and human oversight.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy mandates AI systems to explain decisions and actions and undergo ethical reviews when high-risk.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy instructs employees to ensure data protection and adhere to cybersecurity measures per the Statewide Information Security Manual and NIST-800-53 standard.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy requires informing users about AI interactions and data handling.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy assigns Agency heads responsibility for policy adherence, with AI technologies reported to the Business Relationship Management Division.

State of New Hampshire Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies Policy references New Hampshire AI ethics code and laws related to deepfakes and AI use.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 establishes the Artificial Intelligence Task Force responsible for studying AI technologies' societal impacts and recommending government actions for ethical use.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 includes the Chief Technology Officer, Chief Innovation Officer, Chief Executive Officer of the Economic Development Authority, and other key officials as members.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 authorizes the Task Force to gather data from state departments and agencies.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 requires executive branch cooperation and assistance to fulfill the Task Force's objectives.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 directs the Task Force to consult with academics, industry professionals, and consumer advocates.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 issues a reporting requirement to the Governor within 12 months of the Order’s enactment, to be shared with the Legislature and public.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 permits additional appointments by the Governor as necessary.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 clarifies the Task Force’s advisory nature in providing advice to the Governor and executive branches.

New Jersey Executive Order No. 346 takes effect immediately upon issuance.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 establishes a single state data governance structure, creating a federated data platform to manage data effectively across Rhode Island state agencies.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 mandates the Department of Administration (DOA) to appoint a Chief Data Officer (CDO) to oversee the Data Center of Excellence, enhancing data operations and readiness for AI integration.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 creates an AI Center of Excellence to formulate AI policies and ethics, minimizing bias and guiding AI implementation in state operations.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 directs all state agencies to participate in the federated data system, sharing data for policy analysis and exploring AI applications to improve operations.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 forms an AI Task Force to assess AI risks and opportunities, providing advice to policymakers.

Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06 instructs the Department of Labor and Training (DLT), Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE), and Office of Post Secondary Commissioner (OPC) to develop AI training programs for state and private-sector workers, integrating AI topics into existing curricula.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 establishes an Artificial Intelligence in Education Task Force in Mississippi to evaluate and recommend AI applications in K-12 education.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 requires the State Superintendent of Education to chair the task force, with administrative support provided by the Department of Education.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 comprises twelve members appointed by the Governor, Lieutenant Governor, and Speaker of the House, possessing expertise in education, technology, and data privacy.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 instructs the task force to assess AI's ethical, legal, and data privacy implications, develop policy recommendations, and propose guidelines for AI integration in education.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 tasks the force with identifying workforce needs and strategies for data protection, and fostering collaboration between educational sectors and industries.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 requires submission of interim and final reports detailing findings and recommendations to state officials and public posting of the final report.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2062 dissolves the task force on January 1, 2025, and takes effect on July 1, 2024.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) requires healthcare entities in California using AI to comply with existing state laws related to consumer protection, civil rights, competition, and data privacy.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) prohibits the use of AI to deny health insurance claims or make medical decisions that override licensed care providers’ determinations.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) prohibits the use of AI systems that discriminate against patients based on historical access to healthcare.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) demands transparency and auditing of AI systems, ensuring they do not introduce bias or replicate human error.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) insists that entities uphold patient privacy, especially regarding sensitive information like reproductive and genetic data.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) mandates informed consent from patients when AI tools impact their healthcare.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) outlines existing protections under laws like California’s Unfair Competition Law, Unruh Civil Rights Act, and Confidentiality of Medical Information Act.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) instructs healthcare AI developers to prevent discriminatory impacts and consider the effects of training data.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) emphasizes the need for compliance with both state and federal regulations with no exceptions for AI-related practices.

Legal Advisory on the Application of Existing California Law to Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare (California Attorney General) prohibits the involvement of AI as a defense to liability under any law.

New York 2025-A768 enacts the New York Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Act to manage risks of  AI decision systems.

New York 2025-A768 requires developers to ensure systems do not cause algorithmic discrimination through regular audits, starting January 2027.

New York 2025-A768 mandates developers provide comprehensive technical documentation and risk assessments to deployers.

New York 2025-A768 obligates deployers to notify consumers when high-risk AI systems make significant decisions affecting them and to offer explanation and recourse for adverse decisions.

New York 2025-A768 imposes a risk management program for deployers to identify and mitigate potential discrimination.

New York 2025-A768 allows the attorney general to enforce compliance through audits and penalties, with the possibility of corrective actions to avoid litigation.

New York 2025-A768 establishes exceptions for preempting federal law compliance and protects trade secrets from disclosure.

Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence requires federal agencies to appoint a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) within 60 days to enhance AI governance and innovation while managing risks, particularly those affecting public rights and safety.

Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence requires agencies to develop AI strategies to responsibly adopt AI, including generative AI, and to facilitate sharing and reuse of AI models, code, and data.

Advancing Governance, Innovation, and Risk Management for Agency Use of Artificial Intelligence imposes new requirements for agencies to manage AI-related risks, including following minimum risk management practices for AI impacting public rights and safety. Obligates agencies to annually inventory AI use cases, identifying those impacting rights and safety, and to report on associated risks and mitigation strategies. Encourages removing barriers to AI innovation related to IT infrastructure, data, and workforce while ensuring compliance with existing federal policies and risk management practices.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government directs agencies to improve responsible AI acquisition, emphasizing cross-functional and interagency collaboration, risk management, and market competitiveness.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government requires agencies to update acquisition policies to reflect AI governance responsibilities and share AI acquisition information across the executive branch.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government mandates compliance with risk management practices for AI impacting rights or safety, including managing privacy, security, and discrimination risks.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government urges agencies to prevent vendor lock-in by prioritizing interoperability, transparency, and innovative acquisition practices.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government encourages the acquisition of generative AI for experimentation, while emphasizing transparency, risk mitigation, and environmental considerations.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government applies to all federal agencies, excluding the Intelligence Community and National Security Systems, and sets specific deadlines for compliance and reporting.

Advancing the Responsible Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government fosters a diverse AI marketplace by minimizing vendor lock-in and promoting competition through strategic contractual requirements.

Illinois HB 3506 mandates developers to produce, implement, and publish a "safety and security protocol" to respond to critical risks, along with quarterly risk assessment reports.

Illinois HB 3506 defines "critical risk" as deriving from the development or deployment of foundation models in a manner which could cause serious injury, death, or financial loss.

Illinois HB 3506 defines "foundation model" as an AI model applicable to many different contexts and capable of self-supervision in training.

Illinois HB 3506 requires an annual third-party audit to assess compliance with these protocols.

Illinois HB 3506 allows redactions in published documents for protecting trade secrets or public safety, with unredacted versions available to the Attorney General.

Illinois HB 3506 imposes civil penalties up to $1,000,000 for violations, with consideration of the severity and potential materialization of critical risks.

Illinois HB 3506 establishes whistleblower protections and procedures for reporting internal risks related to AI development.

Illinois HB 3506 authorizes the Attorney General to seek injunctive relief if a developer's activities pose imminent threats to public safety.

Illinois HB 3506 emphasizes the cumulative nature of this Act, not limiting duties or remedies under other laws.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics establishes the National Science and Technology Ethics Commission to guide and promote S&T ethics governance, with the Ministry of Science and Technology overseeing daily operations.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics instructs institutes engaged in AI and other sensitive fields to form S&T ethics review committees to address ethical risks independently.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics mandates that stakeholders comply with ethics requirements and enforce rigorous review procedures for S&T involving human and animal subjects.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics requires strict governance and dynamic regulation aligning with China’s national conditions and international trends.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics directs entities, such as local oversight departments and innovation entities, to manage, monitor, and report S&T ethics risks, ensuring agile responses to emerging challenges.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics prompts legislative actions to strengthen legal provisions related to S&T ethics, particularly in AI, by the end of the 14th Five-Year Plan.

Opinions on Strengthening the Governance of Science and Technology Ethics encourages public and local awareness of S&T ethics through education, laying emphasis on both stakeholder compliance and societal benefit.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 establishes an AI Strategic Task Force within the Office of the Governor of Massachusetts to study AI and Generative AI (GenAI) technologies and their impacts on the state.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 charges the Task Force with advising the Governor on making Massachusetts a leader in AI research and development.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 requires the Task Force to identify collaboration opportunities in key industries such as life sciences, healthcare, and finance, and explore public investments in AI.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 advises on AI-related job creation, assessing workforce impacts, and suggesting workforce training.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 recommends policies for responsible AI development, addressing ethical concerns like bias, privacy, and security.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 empowers the Task Force to convene subcommittees for addressing specific AI issues.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 obligates the Task Force to submit a report summarizing its work and recommendations to the Governor.

Massachusetts Executive Order 629 specifies an effective date immediately after issuance until 30 days post-report submission.

Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (5/2/2024) calls on governments and AI actors to invest in AI research and development, focusing on ethics, privacy, and reducing bias.

Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (5/2/2024) advises governments to develop flexible governance environments and adapt policies to facilitate the deployment of AI systems.

Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (5/2/2024) promotes building human capacity and preparing for labor market changes through skills training and fair transitions for workers as AI is deployed.

Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (5/2/2024) urges governments to cooperate internationally to share AI knowledge, establish global technical standards, and promote use of internationally comparable indicators for AI progress.

Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (5/2/2024) instructs the Digital Policy Committee to continue advancing AI governance by developing practical guidance and reporting on the implementation of these recommendations.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint promotes export policies to securely share frontier AI models with allies while limiting exports to adversary nations.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint encourages federal support for AI companies, including sharing national security insights and reducing bureaucratic obstacles for collaboration.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint advocates infrastructure development to support AI, emphasizing chips, data, energy, and talent to maintain US leadership.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint proposes common-sense rules for AI safeguarding public safety while fostering innovation, emphasizing provenance data in AI-generated content, and AI user personalization.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint suggests creating AI Economic Zones and a nationwide AI education strategy to enhance AI ecosystem support and competitiveness.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint envisions a Compact for AI among allies for capital and supply chain access, contrasting Chinese-backed infrastructure projects.

AI in America: OpenAI's Economic Blueprint engages in developing training programs for future AI talent, promoting collaboration between government and industry.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews requires committees in life sciences, medicine, and AI to manage ethics reviews independently and transparently.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews obliges these committees to guide risk assessments, conduct ethics reviews, and manage interdisciplinary membership for unbiased decision-making.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews stipulates S&T ethics reviews to cover data handling, ensuring compliance with relevant data security and personal information laws.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews mandates expert reconsiderations for high-risk emerging technologies, including algorithms and automated decision-making systems.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews empowers MOST to guide overall S&T ethics oversight and manage the information registration platform for ethical review activities.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews allows simplified procedures for low-risk S&T activities and establishes emergency procedures for rapid ethics review during urgent public incidents.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews authorizes corrective measures for violations, including possible penalties and liability for misconduct in S&T ethics.

(Trial) Measures for Science and Technology Ethics Reviews implements from December 1, 2023.

Workforce for AI Trust Act mandates the NSF to conduct outreach to diverse institutions and groups underrepresented in STEM fields for fellowship applicants.

Workforce for AI Trust Act directs the NSF to promote AI-based training and workshops across STEM fields to accelerate scientific discovery and technology development.

Workforce for AI Trust Act requires the integration of diverse disciplinary perspectives in AI research peer review panels.

Workforce for AI Trust Act instructs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support education and workforce development to expand the AI governance workforce, focusing on managing AI-related risks.

Workforce for AI Trust Act mandates NIST to develop technical standards and guidance for AI risk management careers, including mapping, measuring, and validating AI systems.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 enacts the Artificial Intelligence Act to regulate the use of AI in New Mexico, focusing on high-risk AI systems that make consequential decisions.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 requires developers to use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination and disclose known risks to recipients and the state.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 mandates impact assessments for deployers, updating them annually or upon modification of AI systems.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 obliges deployers to notify consumers of AI's role in consequential decisions and provide appeal opportunities for adverse outcomes.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 exempts trade secrets from mandatory disclosure, but requires consumer notification when information is withheld.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 confers enforcement authority to the state department of justice, allowing consumer civil actions for violations.

New Mexico 2025 HB 60 sets the effective date for July 1, 2026, with rulemaking by the state department of justice due by January 1, 2027.

City of Long Beach Data Privacy Guidelines (2021) defines Artificial Intelligence as machines that have the ability to "learn" and "problem solve".

City of Long Beach Data Privacy Guidelines (2021) mandates human review of algorithmic and AI decisions to avoid discrimination, using evidence-based evaluation of potential discriminatory consequences.

City of Long Beach Data Privacy Guidelines (2021) requires training input informed by outcomes from AI or related technologies.

Mississippi Executive Order No. 1584 mandates ITS to evaluate current AI processes and guidelines at state agencies.

Mississippi Executive Order No. 1584 instructs ITS to develop policy recommendations for the responsible use of AI, emphasizing fairness, privacy, security, transparency, and accountability.

Mississippi Executive Order No. 1584 encourages statewide coordination on AI use, enabling ITS to engage with government stakeholders and industry experts for best practices and strategies.

Mississippi Executive Order No. 1584 requires state agencies to cooperate with ITS by completing AI inventories and designating a staff member for AI coordination.

Mississippi Executive Order No. 1584 implements the Executive Order immediately, with provisions to remain effective until amended, superseded, or rescinded.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 establishes the "Frontier Safety Framework" for managing risks of advanced AI, focusing on Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) related to misuse and deceptive alignment.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 outlines CCLs for high-risk domains, including chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear attacks (CBRN), cyber threats, and machine learning R&D, needing security and deployment mitigations.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 mandates regular evaluations of frontier AI models to assess approaching CCLs, employing "early warning evaluations" for proactive risk management.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 specifies mitigations when models near CCLs, using internal and external expertise to develop response plans, emphasizing automated monitoring for deceptive alignment risks.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 describes governance protocols, involving review and approval by corporate bodies like the Google DeepMind AGI Safety Council, and outlines disclosure criteria to government authorities and external organizations.

Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework Version 2.0 plans continual updates to risk modeling, capability assessments, and risk-appropriate actions as AI capabilities evolve.

National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2025 Action Plan (Turkey) launches advanced analytics and AI training for public personnel competence.

Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150 establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI technologies used by Indiana state agencies, assessing their benefits, risks, and impacts on privacy, civil rights, and legal protections.

Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150 requires the Task Force to produce annual reports with findings and recommendations for policies or legislation to govern AI use by state agencies.

Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150 mandates state agencies compile and submit inventories of AI technologies in use or development, detailing vendors, intended use, data security measures, benefits, risks, and financial implications.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems promotes the safe, secure, and trustworthy development of AI by providing voluntary guidance for organizations developing advanced AI systems.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems encourages organizations to identify, evaluate, and mitigate risks across the AI lifecycle, employing diverse testing methods and ensuring traceability through documented development practices.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems urges ongoing monitoring of AI systems post-deployment to identify vulnerabilities and misuse, through collaboration with stakeholders to mitigate risks, while advocating for public reporting and enhanced transparency regarding identified limitations.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems encourages information sharing and incident reporting, as well as the development and disclosure of AI governance and risk management policies among stakeholders to promote safety and trustworthiness.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems recommends robust security controls, including cybersecurity measures and insider threat safeguards, to protect AI system components from unauthorized access.

Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems promotes the development of content authentication mechanisms to identify AI-generated content and the creation of international technical standards for AI development.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends proactive mitigation of risks across the AI lifecycle and investment in physical, cyber, and insider threat security controls.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends the public disclosure of advanced AI systems' capabilities, limitations, and appropriate or inappropriate uses.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends information sharing and reporting of incidents among relevant industry, government, and civil society stakeholders

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends the deployment of content authentication and provenance mechanisms to enable users to identify AI-generated content.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems encourages development of advanced AI systems foremost to address key global challenge in alignment with the UN SDG goals.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends the development and adoption of international technical standards.

Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles for Advanced AI Systems recommends the implementation of personal data privacy and IP protection measures.
