An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. defines an automated decision tool as any tool that uses artificial intelligence to make consequential decisions relating to employment, education, housing, utilities, healthcare and family planning, financial services, criminal justice, legal services, voting, or government benefits.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. bans the use of automated decision tools in ways that result in algorithmic discrimination on the basis of classes protected by state law.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. requires any entity that develops or deploys an automated decision tool to perform an impact assessment on the tool, covering its purpose, outputs, use cases, inputted data, and potential discriminatory impacts, and the monitoring, safeguard measures, and testing conducted to mitigate adverse consequences. The impact assessment must be updated annually and after any significant update to the tool, and be provided to the state's Civil Rights Department.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. requires any entity that deploys an automated decision tool to provide individuals affected by the tool's decisions with a notice that the tool was used and information on the tool's purpose.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. grants all individuals subject to an automated decision tool's decisions the right to instead have those decisions be made by a human, if technically feasible.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. requires automated decision tool developers to provide the tool's deployers with documentation of the tool's limitations, training data, and testing.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. requires the developer or deployer of an automated decision tool to implement a program that governs the foreseeable risks of the tool's use, including designating an employee to monitor the tool and report concerns.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. permits individuals and public attorneys to bring civil action against entities that violate this law, and makes violation of the law punishable by fines.

An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence. exempts entities with fewer than 25 employees using automated decision tools that affect less than 1,000 people per year from some of this law's provisions.

Ethical Norms for the New Generation Artificial Intelligence outlines 18 specific ethical requirements for AI development, which fall under categories of management and governance, R&D, supply, and usage.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management establishes a U.S.-EU Joint Roadmap to advance trustworthy AI and risk management, promoting shared democratic values and human rights.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management encourages risk-based approaches, aligning EU and U.S. methodologies, including the EU AI Act and the U.S. AI Bill of Rights.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management advances shared terminologies and taxonomies to foster interoperability and consistent application of AI risk management concepts.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management promotes leadership and cooperation in international technical standards, supporting transparency, inclusiveness, and innovation.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management develops a shared repository for metrics and methodologies to assess AI trustworthiness and risk management tools.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management analyzes existing tools to identify gaps and support AI standards development.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management implements mechanisms to monitor and measure existing and emerging AI risks, providing a tracker and interoperable tests.

TTC Joint Roadmap on Evaluation and Measurement Tools for Trustworthy AI and Risk Management establishes expert working groups and consultation plans to advance short-term and long-term objectives in AI governance.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") launch AI security standardization work by coordinating a system of AI security standards, focusing on foundational and application-specific research.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") accelerate development of AI security standards in key areas, driven by urgent needs and safety incidents, to address security risks and ethical issues.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") promote the application of AI security standards through pilot mechanisms and collaboration between academia, industry, and research institutions.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") strengthen training for AI security standardization talent by establishing multi-level training programs and fostering collaboration among universities, research institutes, and enterprises.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") participate actively in international AI security standardization by aligning Chinese efforts with global achievements, enhancing China's influence, and facilitating international cooperation.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") establish an early warning mechanism for high-security-risk AI technologies and products, including a catalog of risks and management standards.

Artificial Intelligence Security Standardization White Paper, Section 5 ("Recommendations for AI security standardization work") improve AI security supervision by developing an index evaluation system, enhancing AI supply chain security management, and formulating supportive standards.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) establishes principles of ethics, fairness, transparency, safety, and accountability in AI development and use.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) establishes aims and support measures for AI adoption, infrastructure development and supports data sharing, compute resources, and algorithmic innovation.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) protects intellectual property laws, user privacy rights and encourages applications of energy efficient AI products.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) implements a comprehensive oversight and coordination framework involving multiple government agencies. Mandate compliance with safety and security assessments, especially for critical AI systems.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) provides legal liability structures for violations, including administrative penalties, tort liability, and public interest litigation.

Artificial Intelligence Law of the People’s Republic of China (Draft for Suggestions from Scholars) promotes international cooperation in AI governance and allows for countermeasures against discriminatory foreign actions.

REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) classifies AI systems into unacceptable, high, limited, and minimal risk categories, defining specific regulatory requirements for each category. Requires strict monitoring and quality management for high-risk systems.

REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) establishes transparency and cooperation requirements for general-purpose AI models. Imposes additional risk management and evaluation obligations for general-purpose models with systemic risks.

REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) applies to AI developers and deployers whose systems are used in the EU market, regardless of their physical location, with certain exceptions.

REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) defines regulatory exemptions for free and open-source AI systems, subject to transparency and licensing requirements.

REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act) establishes the European Commission’s AI Office to lead implementation efforts and enforce compliance. Allows significant penalties for violations. Defines additional AI regulatory roles for advisory boards and national-level authorities.

Department of Defense Directive 3000.09 ("Autonomy in weapon systems") establishes Department of Defense policy on the development and use of autonomous and semi-autonomous weapons systems, including armed platforms that are remotely operated or operated by onboard personnel. Those policies include:

Department of Defense Directive 3000.09 ("Autonomy in weapon systems") requires  testing and evaluation requirements that must be met before a weapons system is deployed, including testing designed to ensure that weapons systems operate as intended even when subject to actions from adversaries. Outlines requirements that humans be able to intervene should weapons systems begin to operate in unintended ways. Establishes guidelines for the use of autonomous weapons systems designed to mitigate the probability and consequences of weapons systems acting in unintended ways.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services establishes legal framework for the use and governance of generative AI services in mainland China, promoting innovation while ensuring security and compliance with national values.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services applies to public generative AI services generating text, images, audio, video, but excludes non-public research and development.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services mandates adherence to laws, ethical standards, and the protection of intellectual property, personal information, and societal values.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services encourages independent innovation and international cooperation in AI technology, emphasizing lawful data handling and quality improvement.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services requires providers to ensure information security, sign service agreements with users, and prevent misuse by minors and illegal activities.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services obligates providers to label AI-generated content, maintain service stability, and establish complaint mechanisms.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services imposes oversight by relevant state departments, requiring security assessments for AI with social mobilization potential.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services specifies penalties for non-compliance, including warnings, service suspension, and legal action for serious violations.

Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services takes effect on August 15, 2023, with provisions for foreign investment compliance.

Global AI Governance Initiative calls on countries to enhance information exchange and technological cooperation for AI governance, focusing on security, reliability, and equity.

Global AI Governance Initiative opposes using AI for manipulating public opinion, spreading disinformation, or interfering in other nations' affairs.

Global AI Governance Initiative urges adherence to international laws and prevention of AI misuse by malicious actors.

Global AI Governance Initiative emphasizes global collaboration to make AI technologies open-source and accessible, resisting technological monopolies.

Global AI Governance Initiative promotes testing and assessment systems for AI based on risk levels, ensuring AI remains under human control.

Global AI Governance Initiative advocates for laws ensuring privacy and data security, opposing illegal data practices.

Global AI Governance Initiative stresses fairness and non-discrimination in AI development processes.

Global AI Governance Initiative calls for ethical principles and accountability mechanisms, addressing ethical concerns timely.

Global AI Governance Initiative encourages wide participation and consensus-based decision-making in AI governance.

Global AI Governance Initiative seeks increased representation of developing countries in global AI governance.

Global AI Governance Initiative supports UN discussions for an international AI governing institution.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to oversee AI advancements and enforce the forthcoming Regulation on AI.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office mandates the Office to develop tools and methodologies for evaluating general-purpose AI models, monitor AI market evolution, and investigate potential regulation infringements.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office requires collaboration with stakeholders, including the scientific community and AI developers, to advance best practices and codes of conduct.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office coordinates with national authorities and EU bodies to ensure uniform application and enforcement of AI regulations.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office supports international cooperation and the promotion of the EU's approach to trustworthy AI.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office tasks the Office with assisting the Commission in preparing relevant decisions and facilitating the uniform application of AI regulations.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office finances the Office through redeployment of resources from the Directorate-General and the Digital Europe Programme.

Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office enters into force on 21 February 2024.

White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Standardization 2021 carry out pilot demonstrations to strengthen AI standardization promotion by selecting national innovation zones for standard application demonstrations.

White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Standardization 2021 create de facto standards to enhance industry competitiveness by promoting AI standards through large-scale applications and integrating them into major projects and open-source communities.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) prohibits the use of GenAI for data classified as SENSITIVE or higher, and personal information should not be input into external GenAI tools.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) recommends agencies avoid using GenAI for business-critical information, systems, or public-facing channels due to risks of inaccuracy and bias.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) advises against using GenAI as Shadow IT, emphasizing the need for robust governance and accountability in AI application.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) encourages agencies to develop GenAI policies, ensuring ethical use, and promoting transparency and accountability.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) emphasizes the importance of considering privacy risks, recommending privacy impact assessments and engagement with Māori communities regarding Māori data.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) warns of security risks, including insecure code generation and data spills, advising strong cybersecurity practices.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) urges agencies to remain transparent about GenAI usage, ensure human oversight, and validate AI outputs for accuracy.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) suggests using sandboxes for testing GenAI safely and advises on procurement principles to mitigate vendor-related risks.

Initial advice on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the public service (New Zealand) this guidance serves as an interim measure while longer-term AI regulatory frameworks are developed.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance mandates embedding ethical requirements throughout scientific and technological activities, including AI, ensuring responsible innovation.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance requires adherence to rule of law in ethics governance, constructing a legal system for AI ethics.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance promotes agile governance for AI, dynamically adjusting to ethical challenges and risks.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance emphasizes the importance of openness and cooperation in global AI ethics governance.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance directs institutions to establish ethics committees for AI and sensitive areas, ensuring compliance with ethical standards.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance urges development of norms and guidelines for AI ethics, enhancing transparency and stakeholder participation.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance establishes the National Committee for Ethics in Science and Technology to guide AI ethics governance.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance mandates strict review and regulation of AI ethics, including risk assessment and compliance with international standards.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance calls for monitoring and early-warning systems for ethical risks in AI, ensuring rapid response to challenges.

Opinion on Strengthening Science and Technology Ethics Governance requires education and training on AI ethics for scientific personnel, raising awareness and ensuring adherence to ethical standards.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") regulates international and interprovincial trade in AI systems by establishing common requirements for design, development, and use.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") prohibits conduct related to AI systems that may cause serious harm to individuals or their interests.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") defines a "high-impact system" as an AI system meeting criteria established by regulations, requiring special assessments and risk mitigation measures.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") mandates responsible persons to assess AI systems, establish risk mitigation measures, and keep records, particularly for high-impact systems.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") requires publication of system descriptions and risk mitigation measures on publicly available websites for high-impact systems.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") obligates notification to the Minister if a high-impact system causes or likely causes material harm.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") empowers the Minister to order audits, require implementation of measures, and impose administrative penalties for non-compliance.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") prohibits possession or use of personal information for AI purposes if obtained unlawfully.

Digital Charter Implementation Act 2022, Part 3 ("Artificial Intelligence and Data Act") imposes offenses for making AI systems available that cause harm or economic loss with severe penalties.

OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta) commits to continually evaluating and forecasting key areas of risk along several Tracked Risk Categories and indicating current pre- and post-mitigation risk in a Scorecard.

OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta) commits to establishing safety baselines where only models with a post-mitigation score of "medium" or below can be deployed and only models with a post-mitigation score of "high" or below can be developed further.

OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta) announces creation of a Safety Advisory Group to assist OpenAI leadership and Board of Directors with making safety decisions by overseeing risk assessments and handling emergency scenarios via fast-track process.

OpenAI Preparedness Framework (Beta) tasks Preparedness team with conducting research, evaluations, and forecasting of risks, submitting regular reports to the Safety Advisory Group, coordinating with other OpenAI teams on recommended mitigations, and managing safety drills and third-party auditing.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper strengthens international security governance on artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies, and prevents and manages potential security risks.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper issues position papers on regulating military applications and strengthening ethical governance of AI.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper stands ready to strengthen communication and exchange with the international community on AI security governance.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper promotes the establishment of an international mechanism for AI governance with broad participation.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper develops governance frameworks, standards, and norms for AI based on extensive consensus.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper encourages responsible bioscience research and adherence to biosecurity guidelines.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper deepens international cooperation in information security, including data security initiatives.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper enhances studies on the impact of emerging technologies on global counter-terrorism efforts.

The Global Security Initiative Concept Paper calls for the formulation of global rules on digital governance that reflect all parties' interests.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence calls for countries to regulate military applications of AI to prevent strategic miscalculation and maintain global stability.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence urges countries to ensure military AI is not used to start wars or pursue dominance, respecting sovereignty and territorial security.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes compliance with international humanitarian law, minimizing collateral damage, and preventing misuse of AI weapons.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence requires human control over AI weapon systems, ensuring data security, and restricting military use of AI data.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence recommends enhancing self-restraint in AI R&D, with accountability mechanisms and operator training.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence stresses the necessity of tiered regulation and risk management to prevent premature use of risky technologies.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence advocates for multilateral dialogue and cooperation to establish a universal governance regime for military AI.

Position Paper of the People’s Republic of China on Regulating Military Applications of Artificial Intelligence encourages developed countries to aid developing nations in governance capacity, opposing ideological divides and ensuring equitable technological advancement.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) calls for governments to prioritize AI ethics by establishing comprehensive rules, norms, and accountability mechanisms.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) emphasizes the need for AI ethical norms, laws, and policies to address potential risks and enhance AI security.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) urges governments to require R&D entities to integrate ethics throughout AI development, ensuring algorithm security, transparency, and data quality.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) prohibits the use of AI technologies that conflict with laws, regulations, and ethical standards; mandates quality monitoring and emergency measures for AI products.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) stresses safeguarding privacy and data security, advocating adherence to international norms for personal information handling.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) encourages public education on AI ethics and emphasizes the importance of public participation and awareness.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) promotes international cooperation to share AI benefits globally, participate in rule-making, and oppose exclusivity in technological development.

Position Paper of the People's Republic of China on Strengthening Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) advocates for international agreements on AI ethics, aiming to establish a widely accepted governance framework and standards respecting national practices.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics establishes a governmental policy framework for AI regulation, emphasizing sector-specific regulation and consistency with international approaches.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics adopts a risk-based approach and promotes incremental development and regulatory experimentation.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics encourages the use of "soft" regulatory tools and multistakeholder cooperation.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics recommends adopting ethical AI principles based on the OECD AI Principles, focusing on growth, human-centric AI, equality, transparency, reliability, and accountability.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics proposes the creation of an AI Policy Coordination Center to advise regulators, promote inter-agency coordination, and lead international representation.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics mandates mapping AI uses and associated challenges in regulated sectors.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics calls for the establishment of forums for regulators and public participation to ensure coordination and open discussions.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics urges active involvement in international forums to develop AI regulation and standards.

Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence: Regulations and Ethics advocates developing tools for responsible AI, including a risk management framework.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit affirms the need for AI to be developed and used safely, human-centrically, and responsibly.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit recognizes AI's transformative potential in public sectors like health and education while addressing risks such as disinformation and misuse.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit welcomes international cooperation to tackle AI risks, emphasizing transparency, fairness, accountability, and human rights protection.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit identifies particular risks with frontier AI, including potential catastrophic harm and manipulation of content.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit resolves to intensify cooperation on AI safety, especially regarding frontier AI, through international collaboration and future AI Safety Summits.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit encourages actors, including nations and companies, to ensure AI safety through testing and monitoring harmful capabilities.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit calls for building risk-based policies and enhancing AI capacity in developing countries.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit supports an international network of scientific research on AI safety and sustains a global dialogue to harness AI benefits responsibly.

The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit commits to further meetings and cooperation to address AI governance, involving countries like the US, EU, China, and others.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services specifies safety requirements for generative AI services in China, focusing on corpus safety, model safety, and safety measures.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services applies to service providers conducting safety assessments and the main oversight department for evaluating generative AI services' safety levels.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services mandates safety assessments and reporting, adherence to cybersecurity, data security, and personal information protection laws.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services requires corpus source safety management, verification, and traceability, including avoiding illegal content and ensuring intellectual property rights compliance.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services demands annotators follow strict training and rule adherence for data annotation and review.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services stipulates model safety, including foundation model registration, content safety monitoring, and ensuring generated content accuracy and reliability.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services outlines safety measures for service transparency, user data collection, and complaint handling.

Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services imposes rigorous safety assessment procedures and compliance for corpus, generated content, and question refusal rates.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality promotes the high-quality development of the AI industry in the municipality by integrating AI with the economy, everyday life, and urban governance.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality defines AI as systems using computers to simulate and expand human intelligence and specifies the AI industry including software and hardware development and application.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality applies regulations to AI-related activities such as innovation, development, and governance within the municipality.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality mandates the Municipal People's Government to lead AI development and integrate AI plans into national economic plans.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality establishes a Municipal Artificial Intelligence Strategy Advisory Expert Committee for strategic advice on AI industry development.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality encourages innovation by citizens and organizations and explores a negative checklist for AI activities.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality supports international cooperation and participation in AI governance.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality encourages AI infrastructure development, including compute resources and big data centers.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality supports algorithm innovation and promotes the trading of algorithm models.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality strengthens AI talent cultivation and promotes AI technology standardization and intellectual property protection.

Regulations for the Promotion of the Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry in Shanghai Municipality implements regulatory measures for AI products, emphasizing ethics and security compliance.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority clarifies that 52 U.S.C. 30124 and 11 CFR 110.16 apply to fraudulent misrepresentation in federal election campaigns, regardless of the technology used, including AI.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority emphasizes that the statute is technology neutral and covers AI-assisted media, forged signatures, and other means of fraudulent activity.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority states that the legal focus is on whether individuals fraudulently represent themselves as acting for a candidate or political party.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority announces that this interpretation will guide the Commission's future actions concerning evolving technologies.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority specifies that this interpretive rule does not require notice and comment procedures, nor does it bind the Commission or public.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Campaign Authority excludes the applicability of the Regulatory Flexibility Act, as the interpretive rule does not involve binding agency action.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence develop advanced AI computational infrastructure and adopt measures to attract top technical talent to work in the United States to ensure innovation and technological superiority in AI.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence instructs relevant agencies to protect AI intellectual property from foreign threats.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence issue guidance on testing and evaluating frontier foundational AI systems to manage safety and security risks.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence directs national security institutions to harness AI to advance national security objectives through clear policies, strategies and coordination, while safeguarding human rights, civil liberties, and privacy.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence produce a strategy for the advancement of international AI governance norms in line with safe, secure, and trustworthy AI, and democratic values.

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence requires covered agencies to appoint Chief AI Officer to managing risks and opportunities of AI

Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence requires the formation of an interagency National Security Coordination Group to harmonize polices related to AI in National Security

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security mandates agencies to identify prohibited and high-impact AI use cases, emphasizing risks to national security, human rights, and civil liberties.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security restricts the use of AI whose output serves as the primary basis for decisions that could pose significant risks to human rights or national security, unless accompanied by human oversight.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security requires agencies to conduct risk assessments and implement minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI uses, ensuring human oversight and accountability.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security mandates annual inventories of high-impact AI use cases and establishes data management policies prioritizing AI systems.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security obligates agencies to appoint Chief AI Officers and establish AI Governance Boards to oversee AI activities and compliance.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security stipulates standardized training for responsible AI use and development, ensuring accountability and documentation.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security allows waivers for certain risk management practices under strict conditions and oversight.

Framework to Advance AI Governance and Risk Management in National Security ensures transparency and public trust through periodic reporting on AI oversight activities, with unclassified information made publicly available where possible.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) amends the title of statute 11.1303 to include synthetic media in political contexts.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) defines "synthetic media" as audio or video content substantially produced by generative AI.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) mandates disclosure in audio communications with synthetic media, stating "Contains content generated by AI" at the start and end.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) requires video communications with synthetic media to display readable notices throughout, indicating AI-generated content.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) authorizes the commission to implement rules, including possible exceptions to disclosure requirements.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) specifies that compliance does not exempt from other civil or criminal liabilities.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) establishes penalties up to $1,000 for intentional violations of disclosure requirements.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) exempts broadcasters from liability unless they are responsible committees.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) clarifies that the act does not alter the rights or obligations under 47 USC 230.

Wisconsin Act 2023-123 (Artificial Intelligence Content Disclosure) applies disclosure requirements to communications created on or after the act's effective date.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) establishes the West Virginia Task Force on Artificial Intelligence within the Office of the Governor.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) specifies membership including representatives from government, industry, education, and health sectors, appointed by various authorities.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) charges the Task Force with responsibilities such as recommending AI definitions for legislation, identifying relevant state agencies for AI policy oversight, and developing best practices for public sector AI use.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) mandates recommendations on AI's impact on employment, protecting individual rights and data, and addressing AI use in education.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) requires the Task Force to assess current AI use in state agencies and consider extending its mandate to keep pace with AI advancements.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) obligates submission of a comprehensive report by July 1, 2025, after which the Task Force terminates.

West Virginia HB 5690 (Artificial Intelligence Task Force) requires initial appointments within 90 days and quarterly meetings, with administrative support provided by the Office of Technology.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media produced by artificial intelligence within 90 days of an election if intended to harm a candidate's reputation or alter voting behavior.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) exempts media with a clear disclaimer that it has been manipulated and includes a citation to the original source.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) classifies violations as a misdemeanor for the first offense and a felony for subsequent offenses within five years.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) allows the attorney general, affected individuals, candidates, or voter organizations to seek permanent injunctive relief in certain courts.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) requires that injunctive relief complaints be non-frivolous and supported by clear and convincing evidence.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) defines "materially deceptive media" as AI-generated content that falsely depicts individuals in misleading ways.

Michigan House Bill 5144 of 2023 (Election Law) conditions the act's effectiveness on the enactment of House Bill No. 5143.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) amends the Campaign Reporting Act to require disclaimers on advertisements containing materially deceptive media created through artificial intelligence (AI).

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) defines "materially deceptive media" as content using AI to falsely depict individuals without consent.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) mandates disclaimers stating the content is AI-manipulated, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media within 90 days before an election if intended to mislead voters, unless accompanied by the required disclaimer.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) establishes penalties for violations: a misdemeanor for a first offense and a fourth-degree felony for subsequent offenses.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) allows enforcement and injunctive relief by the attorney general, district attorneys, affected individuals, candidates, or organizations representing voters' interests.

New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act) excludes certain media types from disclaimer requirements and clarifies non-violation conditions for broadcasting stations and distribution platforms.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) establishes a cause of action for the nonconsensual dissemination of deep fake sexual images in Minnesota, allowing plaintiffs to seek damages, including financial losses and mental anguish.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) defines the crime of using deep fake technology to influence elections, with penalties including imprisonment and fines for violations committed within 90 days before an election.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) criminalizes the intentional dissemination of deep fake images depicting intimate parts or sexual acts without consent, with increased penalties for aggravating factors such as intent to profit or harass.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) allows for injunctions and restraining orders to prevent further harm and includes confidentiality measures for plaintiffs.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) provides exemptions for lawful purposes, such as criminal investigations, reporting unlawful conduct, or scientific research, while ensuring compliance with federal law.

Minnesota HF 1370 (Deepfake Accountability and Public Safety) specifies that these provisions are effective from August 1, 2023, and outlines jurisdiction and venue rules for related legal actions.

Michigan House Bill 5141 amends campaign finance law to require that political advertisements generated substantially by artificial intelligence include a clear and conspicuous statement indicating AI involvement.

Michigan House Bill 5141 mandates that AI-generated political advertisements in graphic form display the statement in large text, while audio communications must audibly disclose AI use at the beginning or end.

Michigan House Bill 5141 requires video advertisements to display the statement for at least four seconds and include an audible disclosure.

Michigan House Bill 5141 imposes fines for violations, with $250 for the first offense and up to $1,000 for subsequent offenses.

Michigan House Bill 5141 exempts bona fide news coverage and platforms with clear policies on AI content disclosure from these requirements.

Michigan House Bill 5141 defines "qualified political advertisement" as including various advertising formats related to elections or ballot questions using AI-generated content.

Michigan House Bill 5141 conditions the act’s effectiveness on the enactment of House Bill No. 5143.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) enacts the "Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act" to regulate synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) defines "synthetic media" as altered audio or video intended to mislead about real events or speech through advanced digital techniques.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) allows candidates misrepresented by synthetic media to seek injunctive relief and damages against the creators or distributors.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) requires disclosures on synthetic media: a visible text or audible notice stating the media is manipulated.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) places the burden on plaintiffs to prove synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) holds information content providers liable, not the medium, unless disclosures are altered or removed.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) encourages courts to resolve cases swiftly.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) declares provisions severable to maintain the act's enforceability if parts are invalidated.

Idaho House Bill 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act) implements the act immediately upon passage due to an emergency declaration.

Utah House Bill 249 (Utah Legal Personhood Amendments) prohibits governmental entities in Utah from granting or recognizing legal personhood for artificial intelligence.

Utah House Bill 249 (Utah Legal Personhood Amendments) restricts legal personhood to human beings and excludes inanimate objects, bodies of water, land, real property, atmospheric gases, astronomical objects, weather, plants, nonhuman animals, or any non-human taxonomic domain.

Utah House Bill 249 (Utah Legal Personhood Amendments) applies these restrictions regardless of other legal provisions.

Utah House Bill 249 (Utah Legal Personhood Amendments) enacts the bill with an effective date of May 1, 2024.

Alabama House Bill 172 prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media, produced by AI, within 90 days before an election if intended to harm a candidate's reputation or influence voting patterns.

Alabama House Bill 172 defines "materially deceptive media" as AI-generated content falsely depicting individuals in actions or speech they did not partake in.

Alabama House Bill 172 allows exceptions if disclaimers clearly state the media's manipulation and provide source citations for edited content.

Alabama House Bill 172 classifies violations as Class A misdemeanors, with repeat offenses within five years as Class D felonies.

Alabama House Bill 172 permits the Attorney General, depicted individuals, candidates, and voter-representing entities to seek permanent injunctive relief against violators.

Alabama House Bill 172 excludes distributors without knowledge of deception or intent to harm from violations, including media entities distributing content as part of legitimate news coverage.

Alabama House Bill 172 protects satire and parody, provided they don't rely on AI for impersonation.

Alabama House Bill 172 effective October 1, 2024.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) establishes a task force in Washington State to assess current AI uses and trends and recommend guidelines and potential legislation for AI systems.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) composes the task force of an executive committee with appointed members from legislative bodies, the attorney general's office, technology experts, industry representatives, and community advocates.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) charges the task force with examining AI development and use, focusing on safety, privacy, and civil rights, and submitting recommendations to the legislature.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) mandates a literature review on AI public policy issues, analysis of existing legal protections, and proposals for ethical AI guidelines and high-risk AI use identification.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) tasks the office of the attorney general with administering the task force, retaining consultants, and supporting subcommittee formation.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) requires the task force to deliver reports to the governor and legislature, with a final report due by July 1, 2026.

Washington Senate Bill 5838 (2024) expires the task force on June 30, 2027.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 mandates that campaign communications using synthetic media include a disclosure stating the manipulation of images, audio, or video.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 allows the Secretary of State and the Attorney General to initiate legal proceedings to prevent violations of the requirement for disclosure in campaign communications using synthetic media.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 imposes a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for violations, with penalties directed to the State Treasury's General Fund.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 excludes certain media providers, broadcasters, and publications from the disclosure requirement, provided they acknowledge potential authenticity issues or involve satire or parody.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 adds the new provisions to Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 260 and amends ORS 260.345 to incorporate enforcement mechanisms for violations involving synthetic media in campaign communications.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 permits the Secretary of State to establish rules to implement these provisions.

Oregon Senate Bill 1571 declares an emergency for immediate enactment to preserve public peace, health, and safety.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) enacts requirements for disclosure of synthetic media generated by AI in election-related communications, effective May 1, 2024.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) mandates audio communications with synthetic audio to state, "Contains content generated by AI," at both the beginning and end.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) requires visual communications with synthetic media to display phrases such as "This content generated by AI" throughout the video or image.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) imposes a requirement for creators and sponsors to include tamper-evident digital content provenance in online advertisements, detailing the creators, edits, and AI usage.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) allows civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) considers the intentional use of AI as an aggravating factor in criminal sentencing, effective July 1, 2024.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) permits judges and parole boards to regard AI-assisted crime as an aggravating factor during sentencing.

Utah Senate Bill 131 Information Technology Act Amendments (2024) maintains judicial discretion in sentencing decisions despite AI-related aggravating factors.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 create the Government Technology Modernization Council within Florida's Department of Management Services to study and monitor new technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI).

Florida Senate Bill 1680 require the council to recommend legislative and administrative actions to promote data modernization and AI system deployment, and establish AI safety standards.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 mandate the council to assess AI's impact on legal rights and its use by governmental and private entities, focusing on potential exploitation by bad actors.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 direct the council to evaluate the need for digital literacy curricula and submit annual recommendations for government technology modernization.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 prohibit knowingly possessing, controlling, or intentionally viewing generated child pornography, with violations constituting a third-degree felony.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 forbid intentionally creating generated child pornography, imposing similar felony penalties.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 prohibit reproduction of generated child pornography in criminal proceedings, ensuring secure custody by law enforcement.

Florida Senate Bill 1680 specify the act's effective date as July 1, 2024.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 establishes the Artificial Intelligence Impact Task Force in Colorado to propose recommendations for protecting consumers and workers from AI systems and automated decision systems.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 defines key terms, including "artificial intelligence system," "automated decision system," and "algorithmic discrimination."

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 requires the task force to consider transparency, disclosure, and protection measures against algorithmic discrimination, and to recommend best practices for ethical and equitable AI usage.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 mandates the task force to include diverse representation and expertise in AI and related fields.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 obligates the task force to meet regularly, with an initial meeting by September 1, 2024, and to submit a report by February 1, 2025.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 permits the task force to continue meeting as needed until its repeal on September 1, 2027, subject to review.

Colorado House Bill 24-1468 specifies that non-legislative task force members serve without compensation, but legislative members receive compensation.

Oregon House Bill 4153 establishes the Task Force on Artificial Intelligence in Oregon, comprising 14 members with diverse expertise.

Oregon House Bill 4153 requires task force members to have proficiency in computer science, AI, technology industries, workforce development, or data privacy.

Oregon House Bill 4153 mandates the task force to examine and define AI-related terms for potential legislation, aligning closely with federal definitions.

Oregon House Bill 4153 requires the task force to gather input from a wide range of stakeholders, including academia, consumer groups, and businesses.

Oregon House Bill 4153 directs the task force to report recommendations to an interim committee by December 1, 2024.

Oregon House Bill 4153 provides that the Legislative Policy and Research Director offers staff support, and state agencies assist the task force.

Oregon House Bill 4153 specifies that the task force ceases on January 1, 2025, with an emergency declared for the act's immediate implementation.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 mandates the Department of Administrative Services to inventory AI systems used by state agencies and make this information publicly available by December 31, 2023, with annual updates.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 requires ongoing assessments of AI systems to prevent unlawful discrimination or disparate impacts, starting February 1, 2024.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 directs the Office of Policy and Management to establish AI policies and procedures for state agencies by February 1, 2024, addressing procurement, implementation, and assessment to avoid discrimination.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 prohibits state agencies from implementing AI systems without impact assessments ensuring non-discrimination.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 establishes a similar framework for the Judicial Department, including inventories, policy development, and assessments.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 prohibits state contracts with businesses unless they comply with specified statutory provisions, effective October 1, 2023.

Connecticut Substitute Senate Bill 1103 creates a working group to recommend ethical AI use in government, assess federal AI guidelines, and propose an AI bill of rights for Connecticut, reporting findings by February 1, 2024.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 prohibits the creation and distribution of deceptive and fraudulent deepfakes of election candidates within ninety days before an election unless there is a clear disclosure that the content is generated by artificial intelligence.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 exempts satire, parody, and interactive computer services from this prohibition.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 imposes a civil penalty for each day a deceptive deepfake is distributed without the required disclosure.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 defines a "creator" as a person using AI or digital technology to generate synthetic media, excluding technology providers.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 clarifies "deceptive and fraudulent deepfake" as synthetic media intended to mislead people about a candidate's actions or statements.

Arizona 2024 Senate Bill 1359 defines "synthetic media" as digitally manipulated images, audio, or video to create realistic but false impressions.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 prohibits state agencies from using AI to classify individuals based on behavior, socio-economic status, or personal characteristics if it results in unlawful discrimination.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 bans real-time and remote biometric identification systems for public surveillance, except by law enforcement with a warrant.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 forbids the use of deepfakes for deceptive or malicious purposes.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 mandates human review of AI-generated, irreversible recommendations or decisions before implementation.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 requires disclosure for content generated by generative AI if not reviewed by a human.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 informs users when interacting with AI systems.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 obligates state agencies to review AI use for compliance within nine months and align procedures with the chapter and ethics code.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 demands removal of prohibited AI systems and ensures new AI deployments comply with regulations.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 directs the Department of Information Technology to report annually on AI systems used by state agencies, noting compliance and changes.

New Hampshire House Bill 1688 specifies the act's effective date as July 1, 2024.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 defines "computer-generated child pornography" to include AI-generated depictions indistinguishable from actual minors engaged in prohibited sexual acts.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 criminalizes possession, distribution, and manufacture of child pornography, including AI-generated content, with varying felony classes and mandatory minimum sentences for first and subsequent offenses.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 prohibits defenses based on consent or mistaken age, but allows an affirmative defense if the depiction is solely of the person charged.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 mandates court assessments for convicted individuals and allows sentence mitigation in specific circumstances.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 requires prior out-of-state convictions for similar offenses to be considered in determining repeat offenses.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 specifies that certain materials with serious value are exempt from these prohibitions.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 incorporates offenses involving child pornography into the definitions of sex crimes, impacting registration and sentencing.

South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79 addresses juvenile sexting, deeming it a misdemeanor if minors distribute or possess nude images or participate in prohibited acts using digital media.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 amends the Indiana Code to add regulations on the use of digitally altered media in elections.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 defines "campaign communication" to include media advocating for or against a candidate, with fabricated media depicting candidates requiring specific disclaimers.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 requires disclaimers for campaign communications containing fabricated media to state that elements have been digitally altered or artificially generated.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 mandates disclaimers in printed, audio, and video formats to meet specific visibility, audibility, and frequency standards.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 allows candidates depicted in fabricated media without the required disclaimer to sue the person who financed, sponsored, or disseminated the communication.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 entitles prevailing plaintiffs to recover actual damages, injunctive relief, and associated legal costs.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 places the burden of proof on the plaintiff to demonstrate depiction in fabricated media by clear and convincing evidence.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 expedites court hearings for related civil actions.

Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133 declares an emergency for the immediate enactment of this regulation.

Maryland House Bill 622 establishes the Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Program in Maryland's Department of Commerce to support small and medium-sized manufacturers in implementing advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, to improve productivity and competitiveness.

Maryland House Bill 622 creates a special, nonlapsing Industry 4.0 Technology Grant Fund to provide financial support, with grants ranging from $25,000 to $500,000, requiring matching funds based on company size.

Maryland House Bill 622 reserves 20% of funds for manufacturers with 50 or fewer employees, allowing unused reserves to be reallocated to larger companies.

Maryland House Bill 622 requires grant recipients to report on fund usage within one year and mandates potential repayment if conditions are unmet.

Maryland House Bill 622 mandates the Governor to allocate $1,000,000 annually from 2024 to 2028 to the Fund.

Maryland House Bill 622 directs the Secretary to establish regulations for program implementation and commence the Act on October 1, 2023.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii) mandates the University of Hawaii to establish a two-year program for developing a wildfire forecast system using artificial intelligence.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii) requires the system to forecast wildfire risks statewide to enhance public safety and improve preparedness and risk mitigation measures.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii) obligates the University of Hawaii to report on the program's effectiveness and provide findings, recommendations, and any proposed legislation to the legislature before the 2026 regular session.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii) appropriates $1,000,000 from the state's general revenues for fiscal year 2024-2025 to fund the development of the wildfire forecast system.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2284 (Relating To A Wildfire Forecast System For Hawaii) specifies that the Act will take effect on July 1, 2024.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 amends Arizona Revised Statutes to prohibit digital impersonation using AI techniques.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 allows candidates or citizens to take legal action against digital impersonation within two years of awareness.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 mandates proof of unauthorized publication and lack of clear indication of impersonation to prevail in court.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 restricts legal action to originators of paid advertisements containing impersonations.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 exempts interactive computer service providers from liability for third-party content.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 permits filing for preliminary declaratory relief in superior court with expedited ruling requirements.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 specifies conditions for granting preliminary relief, such as immediate elections or significant harm.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 allows further injunctive relief and damages for impersonations involving sexual or criminal content.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 sets standards of proof as clear and convincing evidence for relief actions.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 defines "digital impersonation" as AI-manipulated media designed to deceive, excluding parody or artistic expression.

Arizona 2024 House Bill 2394 operates as an emergency measure effective immediately to protect public peace and safety.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference urges extensive discussion on defining and scoping Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems (LAWS), focusing on autonomy levels, human involvement, and distinctions between civilian and military uses.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference advocates for LAWS to be governed by international humanitarian laws, highlighting uncertainties in distinction, proportionality, and accountability with current systems.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference supports developing a legally binding protocol on LAWS, akin to the Protocol on Blinding Laser Weapons, to address legal gaps.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference warns that LAWS increase war's ease and frequency by lowering thresholds and costs, posing risks of indiscriminate harm to civilians.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference calls for caution in using LAWS, particularly to prevent indiscriminate civilian targeting.

The position paper submitted by the Chinese delegation to CCW 5th Review Conference welcomes progress in LAWS discussions within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) framework and supports continued expert meetings.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 prohibits the creation, distribution, or presentation of deepfakes intended to embarrass, harass, entrap, defame, extort, or harm reputations or finances, categorizing such acts as a class B felony.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 establishes an additional offense and liability for legal expenses if the deepfake results in an individual's arrest.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 exempts interactive services, media entities engaged in bona fide news reporting, election communications with appropriate disclaimers, and satire or parody from these prohibitions.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 allows individuals to sue those who knowingly create harmful deepfakes for damages.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 mandates that the secretary of state reject lobbyist registrations from entities convicted of deepfake-related offenses.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 specifies that provisions are severable, ensuring unaffected provisions remain enforceable if any part is invalidated.

New Hampshire House Bill 1432 sets the act's effective date as January 1, 2025, following its approval on July 19, 2024.

Louisiana Senate Bill 6 enacts R.S. 14:73.14 to criminalize the unlawful dissemination or sale of AI-generated images depicting nudity without authorization, with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate.

Louisiana Senate Bill 6 defines the crime as involving images where the distributor knows they lack the authority to distribute or sell the images.

Louisiana Senate Bill 6 exempts interactive computer services and providers of telecommunications or information services from liability if their systems are used for such acts by others.

Louisiana Senate Bill 6 defines "another person" as someone whose recognizable image is used in creating AI-generated content meant to depict a real individual.

Delaware House Bill 333 establishes the Delaware Artificial Intelligence (AI) Commission to make legislative and executive recommendations on AI.

Delaware House Bill 333 mandates the development of statewide AI processes, principles, and guidelines for government agencies.

Delaware House Bill 333 encourages the use of AI in agencies to improve service delivery and ensures AI usage does not violate individual rights.

Delaware House Bill 333 requires an inventory of Generative AI use within state agencies to identify high-risk areas.

Delaware House Bill 333 comprises a 19-member commission, with appointments from state officials, academia, and the private sector.

Delaware House Bill 333 requires the commission to submit an annual report on activities, goals, and policy recommendations.

Delaware House Bill 333 places the commission within the Department of Technology and Information, with staffing support from the Chief Information Officer.

Delaware House Bill 333 sets an expiration of the Act 10 years after enactment unless extended by the General Assembly.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 establishes the Tennessee Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council to guide AI awareness, education, and usage in state government.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 requires the council to submit an action plan to the governor for leveraging AI to improve government service efficiency and capture economic benefits.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 mandates the council to report annually on AI's impact on the labor market, propose legal and policy changes, and recommend workforce development strategies.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 directs the council to submit a final report by December 31, 2028, outlining AI governance frameworks, risk analyses, and recommendations for AI deployment in government.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 requires all state departments to cooperate with the council and allows the council to consult with AI experts.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 specifies that the council members will not receive compensation but will be reimbursed for travel expenses.

Tennessee House Bill 2325 repeals the act on December 31, 2028, and takes effect upon becoming law.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 reappropriates $53,478,000 from the Education Enhancement Fund for fiscal year 2023-2024 to Institutions of Higher Learning, maintaining original funding purposes.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 allocates $15,000,000 to the University of Mississippi for expenses in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, Healthcare Innovation, and related infrastructure.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 limits expenditure to the unexpended balance of funds as of June 30, 2023, and maintains the original purpose of the funds.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 allocates additional funds to Delta State University for flight simulators, Mississippi State University for computing infrastructure, and Alcorn State University for STEM programs, among other specified projects.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 ensures funds support technology transfer and entrepreneurial programs potentially linked to the Department of Defense and related federal research in Mississippi.

Mississippi Senate Bill 3000 requires consistency with the original authorization in Senate Bill 3002 from the 2022 Regular Session.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 mandates the Joint Commission on Technology and Science (JCOTS) to conduct an analysis of artificial intelligence use by public bodies in Virginia.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 requires examination of policies for AI procurement, implementation, and assessment to prevent unlawful discrimination or disparate impact.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 requires public bodies to assess and continually review the impact of AI systems to avoid unlawful outcomes.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 mandates consideration of establishing a Commission on Artificial Intelligence to advise the General Assembly on AI-related issues.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 requires JCOTS to evaluate the composition and duties of this commission based on specified criteria.

Virginia Senate Bill 487 obligates JCOTS to report findings and recommendations to relevant House and Senate committees by December 1, 2024.
