Iowa Senate Bill 2435 promote innovation in areas such as digital agriculture, manufacturing, water quality, vaccine delivery technologies, and biosciences with the allocated funds.

Iowa Senate Bill 2435 ensure that the state board of regents and the institutions of higher learning governed by them do not reduce budgeted funds for their police departments for the fiscal year 2024-2025.

Iowa Senate Bill 2435 require the state board of regents to submit a quarterly financial report to the general assembly, including details on five-year graduation rates for the regents universities in the report for the quarter ending December 31, 2024.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 prohibits the distribution of deepfake content created using artificial intelligence or generative AI within 90 days of an election if it involves candidates, election officials, or parties.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 exempts from the prohibition any media that includes a clear disclosure indicating manipulation by AI, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 allows affected candidates or election officials to seek legal action for injunctive relief or damages.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 excludes liability for platforms providing content from third parties, individuals unaware of deepfake nature, and bona fide news reports questioning the authenticity of materials.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 excludes satire or parody content that doesn't rely on AI.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 requires disclosures to be easily readable or audible based on the media type.

New Hampshire House Bill 1596 specifies the act takes effect on August 1, 2024, with severability of provisions if any are found invalid.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 prohibits the reckless distribution of materially deceptive media, including deepfake and generative AI content, during election periods, to protect candidates' reputations and electoral prospects.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 establishes criminal penalties for violations, including petty misdemeanors, misdemeanors for repeat offenses, and class C felonies for intent to cause violence or harm.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 allows exceptions for broadcasters and online services that did not create the deceptive media, or if disclaimers indicate manipulation.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 mandates that disclaimers must be clearly visible and in the same language as the media, with specific requirements for video, image, and audio content.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 provides civil remedies for individuals or organizations harmed by deceptive media, including damages, attorney's fees, and injunctive relief.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 empowers the attorney general, campaign spending commission, and other authorities to enforce these provisions and seek injunctions.

Hawaii Senate Bill 2687 defines "artificial intelligence" and "materially deceptive media" for clarity and enforcement purposes.

Colorado House Bill 1147 prohibits the distribution of deepfakes concerning candidates for elective office without a clear disclosure, within 60 days before a primary or 90 days before a general election.

Colorado House Bill 1147 requires a disclosure stating the content has been falsified if a deepfake is distributed.

Colorado House Bill 1147 mandates that disclosures in visual and audio communications meet specific size and clarity standards.

Colorado House Bill 1147 allows candidates affected by deepfakes to seek injunctive relief, damages, and other remedies against violators.

Colorado House Bill 1147 exempts bona fide news, satire, and parody from the prohibition, as well as certain media and technology providers.

Colorado House Bill 1147 obligates the Secretary of State to promulgate rules to enforce these provisions.

Colorado House Bill 1147 permits civil penalties and administrative complaints for violations.

Colorado House Bill 1147 establishes the act's effective date as July 1, 2024, with applicability to communications distributed thereafter.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 mandates the board of trustees of the University of Tennessee, the board of regents, and local governing boards of state universities to adopt AI usage policies for students, faculty, and staff by July 1, 2025.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 encourages public higher education institutions to collaborate on policy development and implementation for AI use.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 requires these boards to post policies online and submit them to respective education committees by July 1, 2025, with noncompliance leading to mandatory reporting to the joint government operations committee.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 obliges the adoption of AI policies for students, teachers, and staff in schools by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reports due to the Department of Education starting July 1, 2024.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 instructs public charter schools to implement AI policies by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reporting to the Department of Education beginning July 1, 2024.

Tennessee Senate Bill 1711 takes effect immediately upon becoming law, citing public welfare.

Maryland House Bill 1128 establishes the Talent Innovation Program in the Maryland Department of Labor to increase access to high-quality job training, with a focus on industries such as artificial intelligence.

Maryland House Bill 1128 creates the Talent Innovation Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund to support the program, including job training and talent financing mechanisms.

Maryland House Bill 1128 requires the program to conduct pilots, research, and stakeholder engagement to develop sustainable talent financing approaches.

Maryland House Bill 1128 mandates an initial pilot program focused on the cybersecurity sector to expand regional cyber ranges for job training.

Maryland House Bill 1128 authorizes the Department to provide grants and funding to various entities and individuals for training and support services.

Maryland House Bill 1128 directs the State Treasurer to invest the fund's money, with interest earnings credited to the fund.

Maryland House Bill 1128 compels the Department to adopt regulations and report annually on program activities and fund utilization to state leadership.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 defines "synthetic media" as manipulated images, audio, or video that create a false impression of a real individual's appearance, speech, or conduct.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 allows candidates to seek injunctive relief or damages if their appearance, speech, or conduct is altered using synthetic media in electioneering communications.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 requires disclosure for synthetic media, stating, "This (image/video/audio) has been manipulated," with specific guidelines for visibility and audibility.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 places the burden of proof on plaintiffs to demonstrate synthetic media use by clear and convincing evidence.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 encourages courts to expedite proceedings related to synthetic media disputes.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 holds sponsors, but not mediums, liable unless mediums alter content or remove required disclosures.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 exempts interactive computer services from being treated as publishers of third-party content, except under specific conditions.

Washington Senate Bill 5152 mandates the public disclosure commission to adopt rules supporting this chapter without constituting violations under existing campaign finance laws.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. create the Dyslexia Research Grant Program, administered by the State Department of Education, to support research on AI-based writing assistance for individuals with dyslexia.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. allow privately owned businesses in Nebraska researching AI writing tools for dyslexia to apply for grants, using a prescribed form.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. limit the total grant awards to $500,000, intended to be funded by the Education Future Fund.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. require all grant funds to be used specifically for researching AI tools that use aggregate writing analytics to help develop literacy plans for dyslexic students.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. mandate notification of the Attorney General if grant funds are misused, prompting a civil action to recover funds, which are then credited back to the Education Future Fund.

Nebraska L 1284 (Teacher Incentive Programs), Sec. 2. authorize the State Board of Education to adopt rules and regulations to implement the program.

Idaho House Bill 2472 amends the Managed Care Reform and Patient Rights Act to require utilization review programs using algorithmic automated processes to ensure that only clinical peers make adverse determinations based on medical necessity.

Idaho House Bill 2472 mandates these programs to register with the Department of Insurance every two years and provide proof of compliance with Health Utilization Management Standards or equivalent standards.

Idaho House Bill 2472 requires licensed physicians with relevant board certifications to establish criteria for these automated processes and verify their accuracy.

Idaho House Bill 2472 obliges health care plans to have appeals procedures, allowing appeals to be filed orally or in writing, with decisions rendered within specified timeframes.

Idaho House Bill 2472 ensures confidentiality of patient-specific information obtained during utilization reviews, restricting access to authorized individuals.

Idaho House Bill 2472 permits adverse determination appeals to an external independent review, with potential further appeals to the Department if found arbitrary or capricious.

Idaho House Bill 2472 authorizes the Department to issue corrective actions or cease and desist orders for non-compliance.

New York Senate Bill 1042 amends the penal law to include the unlawful dissemination or publication of intimate images created or altered by digitization.

New York Senate Bill 1042 defines "digitization" as altering an image realistically using other persons' images or computer-generated images.

New York Senate Bill 1042 requires intent to cause harm to the emotional, financial, or physical welfare of another person for the offense to occur.

New York Senate Bill 1042 mandates that the actor knew or should have known that the person depicted did not consent to the dissemination or publication.

New York Senate Bill 1042 repeals subdivision 2-a of section 245.15 of the penal law.

New York Senate Bill 1042 specifies that the act takes effect on the sixtieth day after becoming law.

New York Senate Bill 9678 amends the election law to require disclosure for political communications using materially deceptive media.

New York Senate Bill 9678 mandates visual disclosures to be legibly printed, stating "This (image, video, or audio) has been manipulated."

New York Senate Bill 9678 requires audio disclosures to be stated clearly at the beginning, end, and periodically for messages longer than two minutes.

New York Senate Bill 9678 exempts satire, bona fide news reporting with clear disclosures, stations with consistent disclaimer requirements, and platforms disseminating third-party content in good faith.

New York Senate Bill 9678 permits candidates depicted in deceptive media to seek legal relief, including court costs, attorney fees, and injunctions against unauthorized dissemination.

New York Senate Bill 9678 grants courts authority to provide preliminary relief to plaintiffs likely to succeed in proving violations in upcoming elections.

New York Senate Bill 9678 places the burden of proof on plaintiffs to establish use of deceptive media by clear and convincing evidence.

New York Senate Bill 9678 clarifies that federal law takes precedence over state requirements for media labeling in political communications.

State of Arizona Senate Bill 1565, An Act Amending Sections 16-442, 16-552 and 16-621, Arizona Revised Statutes; Relating to Conduct of Elections. bans the use of artificial intelligence in the hardware or software used to (a) count, process, or adjudicate ballots, or (b) verify voters' affidavits, in Arizona.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" resolves to bridge AI and digital divides globally and promote safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems to achieve Sustainable Development Goals.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" encourages Member States and stakeholders to support regulatory frameworks for responsible AI, fostering innovation and equitable access to benefits.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" calls for cooperation to assist developing countries in accessing AI benefits through capacity building, digital literacy, and infrastructure.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" emphasizes the protection of human rights throughout AI systems' life cycles and urges cessation of AI use that violates international human rights law.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" promotes inclusive governance of AI, addressing global challenges while considering developing countries' needs.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" recognizes data's importance in AI development and urges fair data governance to harness AI potential for sustainable development.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" encourages continued international cooperation, research, and mapping of AI impacts to inform effective governance.

UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development" calls upon UN entities to assess AI challenges and assist developing countries in capacity building for achieving Sustainable Development Goals.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. prohibits entities in Washington D.C. from determining eligibility for, or access to information about, "important life opportunities" (e.g., housing or employment) on the basis of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, familial status, source of income, or disability in a discriminatory manner.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. requires entities to provide a public notice describing any algorithmic tools they use to determine eligibility for, or access to information about, important life opportunities. The notice must be sent to any individual about whom such a determination is made.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. requires the notice described above to cover the data collected by algorithmic tools and how that data is shared externally, how that data informs the tool's decisions, and the rights provided under this act.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. requires entities to provide notice, to any individual against whom they take any adverse action (e.g., firing) on the basis of an algorithmic determination, that the individual may access and submit corrections to any personal information considered by the algorithm. A human must then redo the decision based on the corrected information.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. requires entities to audit their algorithmic decision-making tools before deployment and annually thereafter to analyze discriminatory effects and other impacts, and then implement reasonable measures to address findings of unlawful disparate impact. Entities must submit a report on the audit to the DC government.

A Bill in the District of Columbia to prohibit users of algorithmic decision-making from utilizing algorithmic eligibility determinations in a discriminatory manner, to require corresponding notices to individuals whose personal information is used, and to provide for appropriate means of civil enforcement. permits affected individuals or the DC Attorney General to file a civil action in response to violations of this law, with fines up to $10,000 per violation.

Tennessee House Bill 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children) amends Tennessee Code to include computer-generated images created, adapted, or modified by artificial intelligence under the definition of materials related to the sexual exploitation of children.

Tennessee House Bill 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children) defines "artificial intelligence" as a machine-based system capable of making predictions, recommendations, or decisions, influencing environments, or learning autonomously, developed in any context, including software or hardware, and solving tasks requiring human-like abilities.

Tennessee House Bill 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children) includes "generative artificial intelligence" as a system capable of creating new content or data, such as text, images, audio, or video when prompted.

Tennessee House Bill 2163 (Sexual Exploitation of Children) takes effect on July 1, 2024, for the purpose of public welfare.

Illinois House Bill 4875 amends the Right of Publicity Act in Illinois to define "artificial intelligence" as systems that generate outputs influencing environments, including generative AI.

Illinois House Bill 4875 defines "digital replica" as an electronic representation of an individual created using AI without their actual participation.

Illinois House Bill 4875 prohibits the use of an individual's identity or digital replica for commercial purposes without consent during their lifetime and for 50 years posthumously.

Illinois House Bill 4875 restricts the distribution of works containing unauthorized digital replicas without consent.

Illinois House Bill 4875 exempts certain uses, such as in news, political campaigns, or works of public interest, unless they falsely create the impression of authenticity.

Illinois House Bill 4875 incorporates elements from federal law to exempt certain service providers from liability if they act to remove unauthorized replicas upon gaining knowledge.

Illinois House Bill 4875 applies to acts occurring after January 1, 2025, excluding ongoing or prior legal actions.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee the AI Learning Laboratory Program, which analyzes AI technologies' risks, benefits, and regulatory implications.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 mandates the creation of regulatory mitigation agreements, allowing participants to operate under modified regulations while testing AI technologies.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 sets eligibility requirements for regulatory mitigation, including technical expertise, financial resources, and risk management plans.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 requires participants to report consumer harm, privacy breaches, or unauthorized data usage, with potential removal from the program for violations.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 allows an initial 12-month regulatory mitigation period, with a possible 12-month extension.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 defines using generative AI to commit offenses as a punishable act.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 specifies the program's repeal on May 1, 2025.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70 takes effect on May 1, 2024.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 establishes that using generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a defense against violations of consumer protection laws.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 mandates disclosure when generative AI interacts with a person, requiring clear communication that the interaction is with AI, not a human.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 requires providers of regulated occupations to disclose when generative AI is used in service provision.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 prohibits service provision of regulated occupations via generative AI without meeting legal requirements.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 stipulates that disclosures be made verbally at the start of oral interactions and electronically before written exchanges.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 empowers the Division of Consumer Protection to enforce these provisions, including imposing fines up to $2,500 per violation.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 allows the division to seek court actions, which may result in injunctions, disgorgement of funds, or additional fines.

Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12 permits civil penalties up to $5,000 for violating administrative or court orders, enforceable by the attorney general.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 create the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program to award grants to business entities.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 require the development of AI courses and curricula for K-12 students, emphasizing practical training and career preparation.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 mandate business entities to partner with public or private schools when awarded grants.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 specify application requirements, including program details, school partnerships, and other collaborations.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 evaluate applications based on their potential to achieve program goals and overall viability.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 obligate business entities to enter a written agreement with the office detailing grant specifics before receiving funds.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 authorize the office to establish rules for application procedures, grant awarding, and post-award reporting.

Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13 include an annual written update on the program in the report outlined in Section 63N-1a-306.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 creates the "Road Optimization and Assessment Data Road Pilot Program" to study alternative methods for assessing and financing road maintenance.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 mandates the use of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to evaluate road conditions in Monongalia and Preston Counties.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 requires the Commissioner of Highways to promulgate rules for legislative approval concerning data collection and road assessment.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 instructs the Division of Highways employees to drive all roads in the pilot counties for data capture.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 utilizes GPS, geotagged positioning, and laser measuring systems to assess road geometry and conditions.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 employs video documentation and reflectometer systems for comprehensive road condition analysis.

West Virginia House Bill 3214 requires biannual data capture and processing over three years to track road condition changes and provide predictive maintenance analysis.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 establishes a special legislative commission to study emerging firearm technology, including personalized and microstamp technologies.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 requires the commission to evaluate the risks associated with using digital firearm manufacturing codes for machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 mandates the investigation of the accuracy, effectiveness, and utility of personalized firearm and microstamp technologies.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 instructs the commission to review any legal or constitutional issues relating to these technologies.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 tasks the commission with evaluating the commercial availability of these technologies for new and existing firearms.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 directs the commission to assess the feasibility and utility of a tax incentive program for personalized firearm technology.

Massachusetts House Bill 4885 obliges the commission to submit its study and recommendations, including legislative suggestions, by March 1, 2025.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects administers an artificial intelligence education tool pilot program by the Department of Education for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects awards a grant by the Commissioner of Education for implementing an AI tool in classrooms, involving five selected school districts.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects requires the inclusion of at least one rural, suburban, and urban district, reflecting state diversity.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects mandates compliance of the AI tool with laws on AI use and student data privacy, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects defines "artificial intelligence" as technology using data to train algorithms for tasks usually associated with human intelligence.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects provides professional development for educators in the pilot program, covering AI tool utilization and privacy laws.

An Act Authorizing And Adjusting Bonds Of The State And Concerning Provisions Related To State And Municipal Tax Administration, General Government And School Building Projects trains educators on AI benefits for instruction, student learning, academic achievement, and workforce development.

Utah House Bill 148 amends definitions related to child and vulnerable adult sexual abuse material, including depictions created or modified using computer-generated images.

Utah House Bill 148 defines "distribute" and "produce" in the context of such materials, emphasizing the inclusion of electronic and computer-generated methods.

Utah House Bill 148 criminalizes the distribution of intimate images without consent, outlining penalties, including misdemeanors and felonies for repeat offenses.

Utah House Bill 148 exempts certain entities like law enforcement, legal proceedings, and internet service providers from liability if they incidentally transmit or store such images without intentional engagement.

Utah House Bill 148 addresses sexual extortion, detailing offenses involving coercion through threats to distribute intimate images, with enhanced penalties for aggravated offenses involving children or vulnerable adults.

Utah House Bill 148 prohibits unlawful distribution of counterfeit intimate images, specifying penalties and exemptions for certain entities and situations.

Utah House Bill 148 specifies that the act takes effect on May 1, 2024, providing ample time for stakeholders to comply with the new regulations.

Illinois House Bill 2123 amends the Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act to define terms such as "depicted individual," "consent," and "dissemination."

Illinois House Bill 2123 establishes a cause of action for depicted individuals against those who intentionally disseminate or threaten to disseminate private sexual images without consent, knowing or disregarding the individual's lack of consent and identifiability.

Illinois House Bill 2123 clarifies that consent to creation or previous disclosure of an image does not imply consent to further dissemination.

Illinois House Bill 2123 specifies exceptions to liability, including good faith actions by law enforcement, legal proceedings, and medical contexts, and outlines conditions under which parents or guardians are not liable.

Illinois House Bill 2123 allows prevailing plaintiffs to recover damages, attorney's fees, and seek injunctive relief, while considering factors like age and dissemination scope.

Illinois House Bill 2123 states that disclosure of digitally altered images is not a defense and does not impose liability on interactive computer services for third-party content.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 establishes criminal penalties for wrongful dissemination of deepfakes, defined as realistic digital alterations of images or audio using AI or other technologies, particularly if used to influence elections.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 criminalizes dissemination within 90 days of an election without consent and with intent to harm a candidate or election outcome.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 imposes penalties of up to five years imprisonment or $10,000 fines for violations intended to incite violence or deter voting, with lesser penalties for other cases.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 allows injunctive relief actions by various parties, including the Attorney General and affected candidates, to prevent violations and remove disseminated deepfakes.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 exempts certain broadcasters and publishers, including those involved in bona fide news reporting or satire, from liability.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 requires clear labeling of deepfakes as a defense to prosecution.

Mississippi Senate Bill 2577 takes effect on July 1, 2024.

Indiana House Bill 1047 amends Indiana law to define "computer generated image" as images created or modified through artificial intelligence or software.

Indiana House Bill 1047 prohibits distribution of intimate images without consent, including AI-generated images, categorizing such distribution as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenders.

Indiana House Bill 1047 criminalizes voyeurism involving AI or cameras, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenses or distribution of recorded images.

Indiana House Bill 1047 establishes that using unmanned aerial vehicles to capture private images without consent constitutes remote aerial voyeurism, punishable as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenses or distribution.

Indiana House Bill 1047 exempts certain distributions of images for criminal investigations or under court orders.

Indiana House Bill 1047 requires commencement of actions for child sexual abuse before certain deadlines or conditions, with exceptions for specific bankruptcy proceedings.

Indiana House Bill 1047 declares an emergency for the enactment of these provisions.

Washington House Bill 1999 amends Washington state law to address the creation, possession, and dissemination of fabricated intimate or sexually explicit images using digitization, including artificial intelligence.

Washington House Bill 1999 defines "fabricated depiction" as images altered to show minors or adults engaging in sexual conduct that did not occur.

Washington House Bill 1999 criminalizes disclosing fabricated intimate images without consent, establishing it as a gross misdemeanor or a class C felony for repeat offenders.

Washington House Bill 1999 specifies exemptions for disclosures made in the public interest, such as legal, law enforcement, or medical contexts.

Washington House Bill 1999 clarifies that interactive computer services and telecommunications providers are not liable for third-party content.

Washington House Bill 1999 establishes civil remedies for victims of unauthorized disclosures, including economic, noneconomic, and punitive damages.

Washington House Bill 1999 mandates that fabricated depictions remain in law enforcement custody and are not duplicated during legal proceedings.

Washington House Bill 1999 specifies timelines for filing civil actions related to unauthorized disclosures, especially for minors.

Illinois Senate Bill 382 amends the Civil Remedies for Nonconsensual Dissemination of Private Sexual Images Act to include "digitally altered sexual image" as a defined term, expanding the scope of protection to cover images that are substantially altered to falsely appear authentic.

Illinois Senate Bill 382 specifies that exceptions to liability apply to both private sexual images and digitally altered sexual images, maintaining exceptions for good faith actions by law enforcement, legal proceedings, medical education, and reports of unlawful or unwelcome conduct.

Illinois Senate Bill 382 clarifies that the dissemination of a private or digitally altered sexual image is not a matter of public concern solely because it involves a public figure or is accompanied by a political message.

Illinois Senate Bill 382 retains provisions that a parent or guardian is not liable for dissemination unless done for prohibited purposes, such as sexual gratification or commercial gain.

Illinois Senate Bill 382 establishes that the Act takes effect upon becoming law, without acceleration or delay from previous or other legislative changes.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good recognizes AI safety as a global public good, urging global governance to mitigate risks from advanced AI systems.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good encourages states and AI developers to commit to foundational principles for responsible AI development, fostering cooperation at intergovernmental summits.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good calls for states to establish and resource AI Safety Institutes to advance testing, research, and standards-setting.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good urges development of domestic authorities to detect and respond to AI incidents, coordinating globally for contingency planning.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good proposes Emergency Preparedness Agreements and Institutions for model registration, incident reporting, and contingency plans.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good establishes a Safety Assurance Framework requiring developers to demonstrate AI safety before deployment.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good calls for post-deployment monitoring and independent audits to ensure AI systems' safety.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good calls for independent global AI safety and verification research, funded by a diverse range of stakeholders.

Consensus Statement on AI Safety as a Global Public Good encourages international collaboration to develop verification methods, enabling credible safety claims and fostering trust.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence proposes red lines in AI development and governance development as an international coordination mechanism to prevent catastrophic risks.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence prohibits AI systems from self-replication or improvement without human approval.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence restricts AI from taking actions to increase its power or influence unduly.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence forbids AI systems from aiding in the development of weapons of mass destruction.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence prohibits AI from autonomously executing cyberattacks causing significant harm.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence prevents AI from deceiving designers or regulators about its capabilities.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence calls for comprehensive governance regimes to prevent crossing of red lines.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence requires domestic registration of advanced AI models for government oversight.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence conditions global market access on compliance with internationally aligned regulations.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence encourages multilateral institutions to govern AGI development safely.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence mandates developers demonstrate adherence to red lines through evaluations and proofs.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence urges international collaboration on AI safety research and funding.

Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence emphasizes decisive action combining technical research and governance to mitigate risks.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) encourages governments worldwide to develop measures to prevent worst-case AI outcomes from malicious or careless actors and manage AI safety risks.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) recommends mandatory registration for creating, selling, or using AI models above a certain capability threshold to enhance government visibility into emerging risks.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) encourages governments to implement requirements to monitor large-scale data centers, track AI incidents, and mandate independent third-party audits for AI developers concerning information security and model safety.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) proposes defining clear red lines that, if crossed, mandate immediate termination of an AI system through rapid and safe shut-down procedures.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) urges international cooperation to establish and maintain the capacity to shut down AI systems crossing red lines.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) calls for AI developers to demonstrate to regulators that their systems will not cross defined red lines before deployment.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) advocates for substantial research progress to ensure advanced AI alignment with designers' intent and robustness against malicious actors.

IDAIS-Oxford Statement (2023) encourages a global network of AI safety research and governance institutions, with leading developers committing significant resources to AI safety.
